## 1.1 Purpose

This document is the design and justification record for a **five-bed centralised
Patient Monitoring System (PMS)** for a general critical-care ward. Five instrumented
bedside units feed live physiological data to a single nurse-station hub, which
publishes to the hospital's clinical record, to India's national digital health
exchange, and to the hospital management system.

It answers assignment goals **G1** (ward design), **G2** (centralised monitoring),
**G3** (digital health), **G4** (data modelling) and **G5** (HMS linkage), and
delivers milestones **M1** through **M9**.

## 1.2 What this system is, in standards terms

The classification drives every subsequent decision, so it is stated first.

A 5-bed centralised PMS is a **medical electrical system** built from equipment
governed by **IEC 60601-1:2005+A1:2012+A2:2020 (Ed. 3.2)**, and it is declared for
the **professional healthcare facility environment** of
**IEC 60601-1-2:2014+A1:2020 (Ed. 4.1)**. That single environment declaration selects
the highest of the three immunity tiers and therefore determines the entire EMC
test plan.

The bedside units are **multifunction patient monitors**, governed primarily by
**IEC 80601-2-49:2018+A1:2024 (Ed. 1.1)**. This standard is not named in the
assignment brief, and that omission matters: it is the particular standard written
specifically for equipment of this class, and every other particular standard in the
table below modifies it rather than replaces it.

> *"Where particular standards exist, this standard should not be used alone."*
> — IEC 60601-1 scope

## 1.3 Standard hierarchy applied

| Level | Standard | Edition | Scope in this design |
|---|---|---|---|
| General | IEC 60601-1 | 2005+A1:2012+A2:2020 (Ed. 3.2) | Basic safety and essential performance |
| Collateral — EMC | IEC 60601-1-2 | 2014+A1:2020 (Ed. 4.1) | Immunity and emissions; environment tiers |
| Collateral — alarms | IEC 60601-1-8 | 2006+A1:2012+A2:2020 (Ed. 2.2) | Alarm system; governs the distributed alarm system |
| Collateral — usability | IEC 60601-1-6 | 2010+A1:2013+A2:2020 (Ed. 3.2) | Usability engineering |
| **Particular — monitor** | **IEC 80601-2-49** | **2018+A1:2024 (Ed. 1.1)** | **Multifunction patient monitoring equipment** |
| Particular — ECG | IEC 60601-2-27 | 2011 (Ed. 3.0) | ECG monitoring, not diagnostic reporting |
| Particular — NIBP | IEC 80601-2-30 | 2018 (Ed. 2.0) | Automated sphygmomanometers |
| Particular — SpO₂ | ISO 80601-2-61 | 2026 (Ed. 3.0) | Pulse oximeter equipment |
| Particular — temperature | ISO 80601-2-56 | 2017+A1:2018 (Ed. 2) | Clinical thermometers |
| Software | IEC 62304 | 2006+A1:2015 (Ed. 1.1) | Hub, alarm engine and sync software lifecycle |
| Usability | IEC 62366-1 | 2015+A1:2020 (Ed. 1.1) | Use-related risk of the 5-bed hub interface |
| Risk management | ISO 14971 | 2019 | Top-level risk management |
| Installation | IEC 60364-7-710 | 2021 (Ed. 2.0) | Medical-location electrical installation |

### 1.3.1 Three deliberate deviations from the brief

The brief and the literature it draws on cite standards that are superseded or
misapplied. These corrections are applied deliberately and are flagged here so that
a reader can see each is intentional rather than an oversight.

**IEC 60601-2-25 is the wrong standard for bedside ECG.**
It covers *electrocardiographs for producing diagnostic ECG reports*, and its own
scope excludes *"cardiac monitors covered by IEC 60601-2-27 where not intended for
obtaining electrocardiographic reports for diagnostic purposes."* This system
monitors; it does not issue diagnostic reports. **IEC 60601-2-27:2011 (Ed. 3.0)** is
cited instead. The diagnostic standard is retained in the hierarchy only as the
reference for calibration and gain accuracy, which both share.

**IEC 60601-2-30 no longer exists as a 60601 number.**
Non-invasive blood pressure was renumbered to **IEC 80601-2-30:2018 (Ed. 2.0)**, and
the renumbering also aligned it with the third edition of IEC 60601-1.

**IEC 60601-1-11 does not apply to this project.**
It is triggered by a *home healthcare* intended use, irrespective of operator
training. A staffed general ward is by definition a professional healthcare
facility environment, so citing 60601-1-11 as a requirement would misstate the
design intent. It appears in this document only as the origin of the environment
tier taxonomy that IEC 60601-1-2 harmonises against.

### 1.3.2 Note on the term "De-health"

<!-- lint-allow de-health-typo -->

Milestone M2 asks the team to *"Research Abha ID API and De-health/FHIR standards."*
**No standard, specification or recognised technical term named "De-health" exists.**
The two plausible readings are *Digital health* and *de-identification*. Both are
covered: digital health in section 6, and de-identification and privacy in
sections 6.6 and 8.5. This is flagged as a probable typographical error in the brief.

A second term needs the same treatment. The brief lists *"diathermy"* as a voice of
the customer. Three distinct technologies are described by that word in different
sources — electrosurgery at roughly 500 kHz, short-wave diathermy at 27 MHz, and
therapeutic ultrasound — and they map to **different standards with different
interference physics**. Section 2.6 analyses the electrosurgical case as the
dominant EMI risk to millivolt-level signals, which is the interpretation used
throughout.

## 1.4 Essential performance

For this system the essential performance is not merely the numeric readouts. It is:

1. Accurate measurement of heart rate, arterial oxygen saturation, non-invasive
   blood pressure and body temperature.
2. **Annunciation of an alarm condition** at the nurse station, and its
   acknowledgement by an identified operator — maintained *under disturbance*.

Point 2 is why the alarm path is treated as a safety function throughout this
document and why section 4.4 devotes an end-to-end latency budget to it.

## 1.5 Scope boundaries

| In scope | Out of scope |
|---|---|
| Five instrumented bedside units | Wired or wireless telemetry to off-ward areas |
| Central nurse-station hub, one view station plus a duty-desk repeater | Full EMR replacement |
| RDBMS schema for patients, vitals, alerts, staff and inventory | Clinical decision support |
| ABHA enrolment and ABDM record publication | Live high-frequency streaming to ABDM (see 6.4) |
| Admission, billing and inventory hooks into the HMS | Pharmacy or theatre systems |
| Ward electrical installation and EM zoning | Hospital-wide electrical infrastructure |

<!-- source: report/02_ward_layout.md -->

Goal **G1** requires a safe, functional five-bed layout with instrumented bedside
units. The floor plan is `figures/m3_ward_layout.svg`; electrode placement is
`figures/m3_electrode_12lead.svg` with the derivation reference in Appendix B.

## 2.1 Zoning and dimensions

The ward is 9.6 m by 7.2 m of internal floor area — 69.1 m² over five beds, or
about 13.8 m² per bed including circulation and support space. Beds are arranged in
**three bays** rather than a single row, because bay separation gives a physical
barrier between adjacent patients that a single row cannot.

| Zone | Clearance | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Bed footprint | 2.2 m × 3.0 m | Bed plus head-unit depth and lateral transfer space |
| Foot of bed to circulation | 1.5 m clear | Bed extraction without turning |
| Corridor | 1.8 m clear | Bed transport and emergency egress |
| Bay entry to first bed | 1.2 m | Hand hygiene point before patient contact |
| Nurse station to nearest bay | direct line of sight | see 2.2 |

**Hand-wash basins are placed at every bay entry**, not only at the ward door.
The clinical evidence for hand hygiene is that it is performed at the point of
contact with the patient, not at the point of entry to the room, and in a shared
bay the bay entry is the relevant moment.

## 2.2 Nurse station placement

The station is positioned on the ward's long axis so that **every bed is visible
without the nurse leaving the desk or losing a patient to a corner**. This is not
an aesthetic preference. Under **IEC 62366-1** it is a use-related risk control:
a nurse attending to one patient must be able to retain situational awareness of the
other four without a head turn through an obstruction.

The sightline requirement has a hardware consequence recorded in Appendix A as
**N-04**: bed identity becomes ambiguous the moment a bed is occluded by a curtain,
a mobile screen or a tall piece of equipment. Curtains must not be drawn across a
sightline without the station receiving an explicit indication that a bed is no
longer visible. The bed's `operational_status` field in the relational schema
carries the occupied, unoccupied, closed and out-of-service states that drive this
display.

## 2.3 Bed head services

Each bed head carries the point-of-care services and the monitoring equipment
identified in section 3:

| Service | Specification |
|---|---|
| Multifunction monitor | Wall- or rail-mounted, 5-bed + 1 spare |
| Oxygen | Wall outlet, flowmeter |
| Suction | Wall outlet, jar, with isolation valve |
| NIBP cuff set | Adult, large adult, paediatric, neonatal |
| SpO₂ probes | Reusable adult clip plus single-patient disposables |
| Temperature probe | Single-patient skin probe, axillary |
| Data outlets | Two isolated outlets per bed, medical IT group |
| Equipotential bonding stud | One per bed head |

**Bed head clearance is kept at 1.5 m** so that a nurse can work at the head of the
bed, where monitoring adjustment, airway access and defibrillation all occur, without
the bed being pushed against a wall.

## 2.4 Cable routing

Every bedside cable run is shown on the floor plan as a **segregated data trunk**
running from the nurse station along a dedicated route, deliberately separated from
mains cabling.

This is a deliberate response to a specific and well-documented failure mode in
hospital installations: twin-and-earth data cable run close to mains provides
**no electromagnetic shielding whatsoever**, because the cable has none. Shielded
twisted-pair in a segregated containment is the minimum acceptable construction.

Two further routing rules follow from section 2.6:

1. **Do not bundle ECG, SpO₂ and NIBP cables into a single trunk run.** Bundling
   dissimilar cable types over long distances is the textbook crosstalk geometry,
   and reactive coupling between them is strongest at low impedance and high current,
   which is exactly the NIBP pump's load signature.
2. **Do not route data trunks past the suction tubing.** Suction is a strong
   mechanical and pneumatic source and will induce microphonic artefact in adjacent
   ECG lead cables.

## 2.5 Electrode choice and placement

Placement is given in full in Appendix B and drawn in
`figures/m3_electrode_12lead.svg`. The ward-scale decision is **five-lead** rather
than twelve-lead at the bedside.

A twelve-lead acquisition requires ten electrodes and, in practice, a trained
technician and a settled patient. It is not a continuous-monitoring configuration;
it is a diagnostic one, which is precisely why IEC 60601-2-25 excludes cardiac
monitors from its scope. A five-lead set adds one precordial electrode, conventionally
V5, and is what actually improves detection of myocardial ischaemia in a monitored
patient. Twelve-lead capability is retained in the hub so that a diagnostic
electrocardiogram can be recorded on demand without moving the patient, and that
recording is governed by the diagnostic standard rather than the monitoring one.

Electrodes are disposable Ag/AgCl with hydrogel. The half-cell potential is
approximately +0.22 V per electrode, and because the offsets are common-mode they
cancel **only if the electrodes are chemically identical**. Mixing electrode types or
ages within one patient is therefore a design constraint on the stores system, not
merely a procurement preference.

## 2.6 Electromagnetic compatibility and the diathermy problem

Goal G1 and milestone M1 both name diathermy as a voice of the customer. As set out
in section 1.3.2, this is treated here as **electrosurgical** interference, which is
the dominant EMI risk to physiological monitoring.

### 2.6.1 Why monitors are the victims

Electrosurgery drives currents above 1 A at a fundamental frequency around 500 kHz,
and radiates harmonics extending into the low megahertz range. It can generate fields
of **40–50 V/m at one metre**, and its historical adaptation as a radar jammer is a
reasonable indication of its power. Shielding cannot fully solve this, because
**the patient is part of the radiating antenna**.

Against that, the signals being measured are small:

| Signal | Typical amplitude |
|---|---|
| Electrocardiogram | **1 mV** |
| Electroencephalogram | 100 µV |
| Electromyogram | 10 µV |
| Evoked potential | 1 µV |

The electrosurgical unit also places **100–400 V of transient voltage directly across
the patient's skin**, from the geometry of current returning through tissue of varying
conductivity. The consequence is that the burst is **rectified at the Ag/AgCl
electrodes**, which demodulates it and injects non-stationary interference *inside* the
electrocardiogram passband rather than outside it where a filter could remove it.
Signal-to-noise ratio during activation falls to roughly −90 dB.

### 2.6.2 Three propagation mechanisms

| Mechanism | Dominant range | Relevance here |
|---|---|---|
| Conduction | Below 30 MHz | **Directly applicable** — electrosurgery at ~500 kHz and short-wave diathermy at 27 MHz both fall in this regime |
| Reactive coupling | Any | Inductive coupling follows high current and low impedance; capacitive follows high voltage and high impedance. Crosstalk appears when dissimilar cables are bundled over distance |
| Radiation | Above 30 MHz | Harmonic content of the fundamental |

### 2.6.3 Mitigations, in order of effectiveness

**Physical separation is the primary control and it is not optional.** The
electrosurgical source is located **outside the ward**, behind a shielded boundary,
which is why it is drawn outside the ward envelope in the floor plan. No amount of
filtering substitutes for distance.

**Passive filtering at the electrode.** Three cascaded single-pole low-pass stages at
100 kHz, 30 kHz and 1 kHz, each in its own shielded compartment to prevent leakage
between stages. These are **passive** rather than active filters precisely because an
active front end would be destroyed by the hundreds of volts present.

**Common-mode rejection.** An instrumentation amplifier with a right-leg-drive
amplifier returning inverted common-mode signal to the reference electrode, fed
through a series resistor greater than 330 kΩ so that drive current stays below
10 µA even in a single fault.

**Optical isolation** between the analogue front end and the digital processing
chain, to remove residual common-mode energy and prevent the monitor from
re-establishing an earth path through the patient.

**Adaptive cancellation.** Least-mean-squares adaptive filtering is preferred to a
fixed notch because the notches remain locked where the interference actually is.
It also has an incidental but real advantage in this jurisdiction: a filter designed
for 60 Hz needs no modification to work on a 50 Hz supply, whereas a fixed 60 Hz notch
on Indian mains leaves the fundamental inside the passband.

### 2.6.4 What the standards do not do for you

A point worth stating plainly, because it is routinely assumed otherwise:

> EMC standards specify performance levels but do not tell a designer or an installer
> how to achieve compliance.

Meeting an immunity test does not protect against a 40–50 V/m electrosurgical field at
one metre. **Formal EM zoning and specified separation distances are the design
controls**; the EMC test result is evidence that they are necessary, not a substitute
for them.

Electrosurgical smoke is a separate occupational hazard requiring evacuation at the
surgical field and is out of scope for this monitoring design, but it is noted because
the smoke evacuator's motor is a large switched inductive load that belongs on a
**separate supply circuit** and should be routed at least two metres from the data
trunk.

## 2.7 Electrical installation

Specified by **IEC 60364-7-710:2021**, which applies to electrical installations in
medical locations.

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Supply grouping | Each bed head is on a designated group. Group 2 (critical) supplies the monitoring outlets. |
| Medical IT system | An isolated, unearthed system with an isolating transformer, providing a first line of defence independent of the earth reference |
| Insulation monitoring | Continuous insulation monitoring to **IEC 61557-8**, with alarm to staff. A first insulation fault must be annunciated before a second develops a dangerous touch voltage |
| Equipotential bonding | A protective bonding conductor at every bed head, reducing touch potential during a first fault |
| Automatic disconnection | RCD selection appropriate to the medical group. Note that residual-current protection is constrained within a medical IT system |
| Essential supply | Changeover to a battery-supported safety supply for the critical group |

The five bonding studs marked EPS-01 to EPS-05 on the floor plan are the physical
realisation of this requirement, and each is recorded against its bed in the `beds`
table as `bonding_stud_id` so that the record can be traced to the installation
rather than to a drawing nobody maintains.

## 2.8 Environmental conditions

The ward operates within 10–35 °C and 10–90 % relative humidity. Equipment rated to
that envelope is specified, and the ward has no local heating, cooling or humidity
control beyond the building services — an assumption recorded because it constrains
equipment selection and would need revisiting in any ward with dedicated conditioning.

<!-- source: report/03_instrument_specs.md -->

The brief asks for each bedside device to be specified by signal type, power
rating and isolation class. This section provides those, and additionally
records the measurement physics, because the accuracy figures in any
specification table are only meaningful alongside the method that produced
them.

**A framing that governs the whole section:** all four measurements are
estimations from indirect proxies, not direct measurements. Mean arterial
pressure is inferred from the shape of an oscillogram. Oxygen saturation is
inferred from a ratio of absorbances through a scattering tissue bed. The
strongest engineering content available here is therefore not the numbers but
the error budgets behind them.

## 3.1 Summary specification table

| | **ECG** | **NIBP** | **SpO₂** | **Body temperature** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Signal type** | Surface electrical potential, DC-coupled | Pressure oscillations superimposed on a cuff ramp | Optical transmittance, two wavelengths | Resistive (NTC thermistor) |
| **Amplitude** | ~1 mV against ±300 mV electrode offset | AC 0.1–10 % of a 0–300 mmHg DC ramp | AC ≈ 0.01–10 % of DC | NTC ≈ 10 kΩ @ 25 °C |
| **Principle** | Differential amplification across Einthoven / Wilson terminals | Cuff occludes artery and acts as transducer | Beer–Lambert, ratio-of-ratios | Steinhart–Hart R–T conversion |
| **Bandwidth** | 0.5–40 Hz monitoring | DC to ~40 Hz envelope | ~1–5 Hz pulse | 0.1–10 s response |
| **Accuracy** | Gain ±5 % | Mean ≤ 5 mmHg, SD ≤ 8 mmHg | ±2 % over 70–100 % | Lab ≤ ±0.3 °C |
| **Applied part** | **Type CF, defibrillation-proof** | Type BF | Type BF, defib-proof | Type BF |
| **Isolation barrier** | 2 MOPP, 4 kV RMS / 1 min | 2 MOPP, 4 kV RMS / 1 min | 2 MOPP, 4 kV RMS / 1 min | 2 MOPP, 4 kV RMS / 1 min |
| **Patient leakage (normal)** | 10 µA | 100 µA | 100 µA | 100 µA |
| **Supply** | 100–240 V AC → 12 V bus | same, plus pneumatic drive | same, isolated sensor rail | same, low current |
| **Power (whole monitor)** | 60–100 W design figure | — | — | — |
| **Standard** | IEC 60601-2-27 | IEC 80601-2-30 | ISO 80601-2-61 | ISO 80601-2-56 |

## 3.2 Isolation architecture — the central design decision

Under **IEC 80601-2-49** the design must choose between two arrangements, and the
choice determines whether the standard is tractable to demonstrate.

A *single function* is the measurement of one physiological parameter. The
standard permits **one applied part carrying multiple single functions** that all
share a single circuit reference. It also permits **multiple separate applied
parts**, each independently isolated.

The first arrangement creates **potential leakage-current paths between single
functions** — ECG, SpO₂, NIBP and temperature all referenced to one common point —
which must each be tested. The testing asymmetry makes the second arrangement far
more practical: for a Type BF applied part all patient connections are tied
together at one measurement point, but for **Type CF each patient connection is
measured individually**, because the limit is ten times tighter.

> **Design decision: each bed's ECG forms its own isolated Type CF domain, with
> SpO₂, NIBP and temperature on a separately isolated Type BF domain.**

This makes 80601-2-49 compliance demonstrable module by module and allows a
parameter module to be hot-swapped without re-testing the entire patient
connection.

The applied-part assignment follows from this:

| Applied part | Class | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| ECG electrodes and lead wires | **Type CF, defibrillation-proof** | Chest electrodes on a patient with an intracardiac catheter or surgical chest access are effectively direct cardiac application |
| SpO₂ probe | Type BF, defibrillation-proof | Non-invasive, not applied to the heart |
| NIBP cuff and hose | Type BF | Non-invasive, limb |
| Temperature probe | Type BF | Non-invasive |

The Type CF limit is ten times tighter than Type BF for a stated reason:
**34 µA rms at 50 or 60 Hz through the heart can compromise cardiac function.**
That figure is the physiological threshold, and it is what makes the ECG
barrier a design constraint rather than a compliance formality.

## 3.3 ECG

**Working principle.** The myocardium acts as a volume current dipole, producing
body-surface potentials of order 0.5–4 mV. Each electrode–electrolyte interface
presents a DC half-cell potential of about +0.22 V for Ag/AgCl. These offsets are
common-mode and self-cancelling *only if the electrodes are chemically identical*.
The resulting input DC offset is therefore typically ±300 mV against a 1–2 mV
signal: **a dynamic-range problem of 100–300 dB**, and the defining engineering
constraint of the ECG front end.

**Front-end chain.**

```
electrode → DC blocking → instrumentation amplifier → right-leg drive
          → anti-ESU filter → 24-bit ADC → digital filter → display
```

| Parameter | Design value |
|---|---|
| Electrode–skin impedance target | ≤ 5 kΩ per junction |
| Alarm threshold on electrode impedance | > 30 kΩ |
| DC current into patient leads | ≤ 0.1 µA |
| System noise, referred to input | ≤ 30 µV p-p over 10 s |
| Common-mode rejection, system test | ≤ 1 mV p-p for 20 V rms at 50 Hz injected through 100 pF |
| Right-leg-drive series resistor | > 330 kΩ, to hold RLD current < 10 µA even in single fault |

**A note on the mains notch.** India's supply is 50 Hz, so the notch must be
set to 50 Hz, not 60 Hz. This is a small specification line with a large
practical consequence: a 60 Hz notch leaves the fundamental mains component
inside the ECG passband.

**Calibration.** The full standard is **10 mm/mV**; fixed gains of 20, 10 and
5 mm/mV are selectable, with ±5 % gain accuracy. The commonly quoted
**5 mm/mV is half-standardisation** — the same thing as "0.5 mV/cm", and it
is a display choice, not the standard gain.

**Bandwidth and its bench test.** Diagnostic bandwidth is 0.05–150 Hz, verified
by a 20 ms triangular wave showing at most 12 % amplitude reduction. Monitoring
bandwidth is 0.5–40 Hz, verified by a 40 ms triangular wave allowing 30 %
reduction.

> **Design decision: the system defaults to monitoring bandwidth
> (0.5–40 Hz) with a hardware baseline-reset function, and the diagnostic mode
> is labelled as not defibrillation-certified.**

The reason is a recovery-time problem. A 0.05 Hz high-pass has a 20 s time
constant. After a defibrillator pulse of roughly 1000× normal signal amplitude,
the trace can take 10–15 s to become visible again, with residual offsets of
5–50 mV. Monitors commonly pass the defibrillation-recovery test with the
monitoring filter and fail with the diagnostic filter, and the standards do not
mandate which filter is used. Making baseline reset independent of filter
selection is a risk-management requirement, not a convenience.

**Cabling.** Trunk cables are proprietary and **not interchangeable** between
vendors. Both the AHA and IEC electrode colour conventions remain in service, so
the chosen convention must be stated explicitly or the wrong leadwires will be
purchased. A published manufacturer recall covering 58,045 trunk cables
worldwide for reducing delivered defibrillation energy leads to one requirement:
**defibrillation-proof patient cables, not merely defibrillation-proof
electrodes.**

## 3.4 NIBP

Oscillometric measurement has replaced auscultation because it removes the human
observer, works in noisy environments, and is fully automatable. The standard is
explicit that the device **does not measure blood pressure — it estimates it.**

Mean arterial pressure is the cuff pressure at peak envelope amplitude, where
transmural arterial pressure passes through zero. **Systolic and diastolic have
no physical marker** and are inferred from envelope shape by a proprietary
algorithm:

| Algorithm | Basis | Performance |
|---|---|---|
| Maximal amplitude | MAP from envelope peak, then ratios | Peak is closer to 0.45·SBP + 0.55·DBP than to MAP; total error typically 10–15 % |
| Fixed ratio | ~0.50 of maximum on the descending branch for SBP, ~0.70 ascending for DBP | Brittle; true ratios vary over 0.5–0.6, and a ratio error of 0.2 amplifies into a pressure error of more than 40× |
| Derivative | Track d(amplitude)/d(cuff pressure) | Under 1.5 mmHg if oscillogram noise is removed |

> **Stated limitation: NIBP accuracy has no independently verifiable systolic or
> diastolic reference. It is validated as a system against a reference device,
> never derived analytically.**

**Accuracy criterion** (ISO 81060-2): mean difference ≤ 5 mmHg, SD ≤ 8 mmHg,
85 subjects, every cuff size tested. Real-world critical-care performance is
narrower than this suggests: a 2022 systematic review across 1,593 patients found
a pooled mean-arterial-pressure bias of −1.50 mmHg, which is clinically
acceptable, but 95 % limits of agreement spanning −14.6 to +40.3 mmHg. **The
limits of agreement, not the bias, determine whether the device is usable during
vasopressor titration.**

**Cuff sizing dominates real-world error.** Bladder width should be 40 % of arm
circumference and length 80 %. A wrongly sized cuff can shift the result by up to
30 mmHg — six times the standard's own mean-error criterion. Adult size covers
23–33 cm of limb circumference. **IEC 80601-2-30 caps neonatal cuff pressure at
150 mmHg**, so a separate neonatal mode is mandatory.

**Pneumatic and timing.** Cuff range 0–300 mmHg, inflation 20–60 mmHg/s, and a
measurement-phase **deflation rate of 2–4 mmHg/s** — far slower than the
inflation rate, because the oscillogram must be sampled along the pressure axis.
Fast or static mode runs 5–10 mmHg/s as a deliberate compromise. A typical adult
measurement therefore takes 30–60 s.

**Electrosurgical interference recovery is mandatory essential performance**
(IEC 80601-2-30). The NIBP module must recover from ESU bursts; this is not an
optional robustness feature.

## 3.5 SpO₂

Two wavelengths are used: 660 nm and 940 nm. Between 600 and 800 nm
deoxyhaemoglobin absorbs far more strongly than oxyhaemoglobin; above 800 nm the
relationship reverses. That spectral inversion is the entire physical basis.

SpO₂ is derived from the ratio of ratios R, mapped through an empirically fitted
quadratic curve `aR² + bR + c`. The curve comes from **controlled desaturation
studies on healthy volunteers**, with arterial saturation measured *in vitro by
co-oximetry*. It is not transferable between sensor geometries — a different
optical shield on the same sensor shifts the curve.

**Validation requirement** (ISO 80601-2-61): at least 200 paired observations
evenly distributed over 70–100 % SaO₂, on at least 10 subjects spanning age and
gender and a range of skin pigmentation, using 10–12 stable plateaus.

**Why the reading is wrong when it is wrong:**

| Failure mode | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| 70–85 % range | The steep part of the curve has the least supporting physiological and optical data |
| Carbonmonoxyhaemoglobin | Two wavelengths physically cannot distinguish it. Reads as oxyhaemoglobin — **a carbon-monoxide-poisoned patient can display 100 %** |
| Methaemoglobinaemia | Absorbs broadly, driving readings toward ~85 % — the "saturation gap" |
| Low perfusion | The pulsatile component collapses into the noise floor; ~0.3 % modulation is the practical limit |
| Motion | Shifts the optical path and phase, corrupting both AC and DC estimates |
| Dyes and inks | Methylene blue, indocyanine green and henna all bias the reading |
| Darker skin pigmentation | Overestimation, now an explicit regulatory concern |
| Optical path-length ratio | The fundamental limit: Beer–Lambert assumes no scattering, but tissue scatters heavily and the scattering constant differs between red and infrared |

**Governance consequence.** A **co-oximeter is required as the arbiter**
whenever carbon monoxide or methaemoglobinaemia is suspected. The monitor
cannot detect these conditions and must not be relied upon to do so.

> **Scope boundary worth recording: ISO 80601-2-61 explicitly does not apply to
> remote or slave equipment displaying SpO₂ outside the patient environment.**
> The nurse-station display of the same reading is therefore outside the scope
> of the oximeter standard and is governed by IEC 80601-2-49 and IEC 60601-1
> instead. The same reasoning applies to every other parameter: the bedside
> module is in scope of its particular standard, the central display is not.

## 3.6 Body temperature

**The regulated requirement is laboratory accuracy against a blackbody, within
±0.3 °C** (ISO 80601-2-56 and ASTM E1965). These standards do **not** specify a
clinical accuracy requirement — they specify laboratory accuracy plus a clinical
comparison study. The per-site figures often quoted are sensor element
tolerances, not the standard's limit.

| Layer | Figure |
|---|---|
| Sensor element tolerance | ±0.1 °C at 37 °C; ±0.2 °C across 5–45 °C |
| **System laboratory error (the standard's requirement)** | **≤ ±0.3 °C** |
| Reported in-hospital probe error | mean 0.04 °C at 37 °C |
| Forehead and ear infrared units | over half failed the laboratory criterion in one survey |

**The clinically important finding is that site matters more than sensor
accuracy.** A systematic review across 13 cohort studies and 105,375
measurements found that axillary, tympanic-infrared and zero-heat-flux
thermometers all **underestimate** intravascular temperature, with only
oesophageal measurement showing clinically acceptable accuracy.

> **Design decision: the monitor ships with an explicit site-offset table keyed
> by site, age band and mode, and the user documentation states that axillary
> skin temperature is a proxy and not core temperature.**

**Probe technology.** An NTC thermistor is selected for sensitivity and cost,
with self-heating as the dominant accuracy risk. The rule that follows is
quantitative rather than qualitative: **bias the probe with a constant current
source at 50–100 µA, not a resistive divider**, and always apply a two-term
Steinhart–Hart conversion. Datasheet curves alone give ±0.26 °C; Steinhart–Hart
gives ±0.03 °C — a ninefold improvement — while linear approximation gives ±1.2 °C.

**Infection control.** Single-patient probes are mandatory for paediatrics,
neonates and immunocompromised patients, and disposable probe covers are
required for any mucosal or ear-canal site. Alcohol disinfection produces a
large transient error and requires 5–10 minutes to settle — a practical cause of
spurious temperature alarms.

## 3.7 Power and internal rails

Mains input is 100–240 V AC, 50/60 Hz universal, Class I with an equipotential
bonding terminal. **The Indian supply is 230 V at 50 Hz.**

Internal distribution, following real monitor service documentation:

```
100-240 VAC ──► [2 MOPP AC/DC PSU, 4 kVrms] ──► 12-15 V DC bus
   ├── +3.3 V   display, CPU, module rack
   ├── +5.0 V   interface, recorder, storage, USB
   ├── +12 V    recorder, display backlight, parameter modules
   └── [isolating DC/DC, 1.5-5 kVac] ──► isolated patient-side rails
```

Design for **60–100 W** per full-featured monitor. Published marketplace figures
for the same product family range from 50 W to 150 W and are not reliable;
manufacturer technical documentation for comparable units sits in the 17.5 W
to 140 W range depending on configuration.

> **Design principle: the patient-facing sensor rail is isolated from mains and
> chassis ground independently of the main power-supply barrier, because the
> sensor cable is the most exposed part of the system.**

This is also the direct architectural argument for a centralised hub. The sensor
bus requires a **second** isolation barrier beyond the power barrier, and a
networked bedside unit cannot be assumed to have it. A central hub that owns
patient-side isolation removes that assumption from the network entirely.

## 3.8 Specification-to-verification matrix

| Specification claim | Verified against |
|---|---|
| Alarm priority values | IEC 60601-1-8 Table 1 — enforced by `ck_alerts_priority` in `db/01_schema.sql` |
| Applied-part classes | IEC 60601-1 and IEC 80601-2-49 — section 3.2 |
| Parameter codes and units | LOINC and UCUM — enforced by `parameters` lookup and `ck_parameters_ucum` |
| MAP is derived, not measured | `ck_vitals_derived_provenance` in `db/01_schema.sql` |
| Physiologically plausible ranges | `ck_vitals_hr_plausible`, `ck_vitals_spo2_plausible`, `ck_vitals_bp_plausible`, `ck_vitals_temp_plausible` |

Section 5.5 shows these constraints being exercised by the build harness rather
than merely asserted here.

<!-- source: report/04_system_architecture.md -->

Goal **G2** requires all five beds to feed live vitals to a single nurse-station hub.
The block diagram is `figures/m4_block_diagram.svg`.

## 4.1 Architecture in one sentence

Five bedside monitors publish over a dedicated segmented network to a hub that
terminates their device associations, normalises terminology, evaluates alarm limits
locally, and serves one nurse station plus a duty-desk repeater — with the archival
record and the national health exchange deliberately kept off the alarm path.

## 4.2 The classification that shapes everything: a distributed alarm system

The single most consequential standards statement in this project is that
**a bedside monitor routing alarms to a nursing station is the canonical example of a
distributed alarm system** under **IEC 60601-1-8**.

A distributed alarm system is one in which the alarm is communicated from the source
device to one or more remote devices for operator awareness. The standard sets
expectations on **reliability, latency, fault indication and single-point-of-failure
analysis** for exactly that arrangement.

This classification is not a formality. It carries four concrete obligations:

1. **Reliability.** An alarm that exists at the bedside and does not appear at the
   station has failed, regardless of whether the physiological alarm was genuine.
2. **Latency.** The standard sets thresholds above which delay statistics must be
   disclosed in the instructions for use. Those thresholds are addressed in 4.4.
3. **Fault indication.** If the network or the hub fails, the system must *say so*
   rather than silently displaying stale data.
4. **Single-point-of-failure analysis.** The hub is a single point of failure for all
   five beds, and must be treated as such in the design and in the risk file.

**The design consequence is the most important architectural decision in this
document: alarm evaluation happens at the bedside and at the hub, and never on the
archival path.** If alarm detection depended on a successful database write, then a
storage fault would become a patient-safety fault. This is why section 6.5 separates
the real-time and archival paths.

## 4.3 Transport and the normalisation gateway

### 4.3.1 Why a gateway is unavoidable

A clinical monitor does not speak FHIR. It speaks a vendor protocol, or an IEEE 11073
device association negotiated at the application layer over a serial or network port.
A FHIR server speaks HTTPS and JSON. **Nothing bridges these natively.** The gateway is
therefore not an implementation convenience but the primary architectural decision.

Beyond translation, the gateway is the **single normalisation point**. Device-specific
codes are mapped to LOINC and UCUM in exactly one place, so that integrating a new
monitor model is a change to one component rather than to every consumer of the data.
This is the translator-and-adapter pattern, and it is the defensible answer at a scale
where the bedside hardware is under the design team's control.

Its scale requirement is real but modest: five beds at one to five updates per second
across ten parameters produces on the order of **50–250 messages per second** at one
station. Ingest is therefore batched per bed rather than written as individual
resources, and full-disclosure waveform data is kept out of the relational store
entirely.

### 4.3.2 Transport choice

| Criterion | FHIR over HTTPS | HL7 v2 over MLLP | MQTT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Offline tolerance | Fails if the server is down | Partial | Queued, replayed on reconnect |
| Acknowledgement | HTTP status | Application-level message | Built into QoS 1 |
| Fan-out | One request per subscriber | Consumer must be addressed | Native |
| Backpressure | Server errors | Application-level | Built in |
| Semantic richness | High | Codes in string fields | None |
| Regulatory recognition | High | Medium | Low |

**Selection: Ethernet for transport, MQTT at QoS 1 for the real-time feed, FHIR R4 over
HTTPS for the durable record, and HL7 v2 only as an input adapter where a specific
monitor cannot be spoken to any other way.**

Two points justify this rather than a single-protocol answer:

- **Ethernet is the only acceptable physical transport for a fixed bedside unit.**
  USB offers no galvanic isolation guarantee and is therefore unsuitable for
  patient-connected data. Wireless is discouraged for a fixed installation: it
  occupies unlicensed spectrum in a building that already runs clinical Wi-Fi.
- **QoS 1 matters specifically.** It provides delivery acknowledgement and replay.
  This is what makes an at-least-once feed safe, and the schema is built to expect it:
  the unique key on instrument, parameter and timestamp means a redelivered sample is
  rejected rather than duplicated. Section 5.5 shows this constraint being exercised.

### 4.3.3 Time synchronisation

The hub is the network time source; all five beds, both view stations and the recorder
synchronise to it at sub-second resolution.

This is not operational tidiness. Alarm thresholds, "time since event" displays,
early-warning-score calculation and waveform alignment all depend on it, and an
alarm timeline that cannot be reconstructed across five beds is worthless for
post-incident review. Every vitals row therefore records **both** the moment the sensor
sampled and the moment the hub wrote the row, so that the transport component of the
latency budget is measurable rather than assumed.

## 4.4 End-to-end alarm latency budget

The distributed-alarm obligation is discharged by stating a budget and then measuring
it. The table below is the design target.

| Stage | Budget | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Sensor acquisition to bedside detection | 0.5–1.0 s | Dominated by signal averaging; the SpO₂ averaging window alone is 8–16 s depending on sensitivity setting |
| Bedside signal generation | ≤ 0.2 s | Includes alarm priority evaluation |
| Network transport | ≤ 0.1 s | Local switched Ethernet |
| Hub receipt and re-annunciation | ≤ 0.3 s | |
| Nurse perception and acknowledgement | 3–20 s | Human, not engineered, but bounded by observation of the display |
| **Total, onset to nurse** | **4–8 s** | |
| **Total, onset to remote annunciation** | **1.5–2.5 s** | |

Two disclosure thresholds in the alarm standard apply to these numbers, and both must
be honoured: where the maximum alarm condition delay plus the maximum signal
generation delay exceeds ten seconds, the statistics of each distribution must be
disclosed in the instructions for use; where the mean delays sum to more than five
seconds, the delays must be disclosed. **This design publishes both sets of figures
rather than relying on being under the threshold**, because a clinically meaningful
alarming rate across five beds will exceed a five-second mean more often than not.

The mean-reverberation time to declare an alarm may additionally be disclosed as the
maximum time to generate the technical alarm condition at a remote location.

### 4.4.1 Two delays that must be disclosed explicitly

**Suppression delay.** Oxygen saturation alarms are suppressed while the
non-invasive blood cuff inflates, because cuff inflation reliably produces a
spurious desaturation artefact. This is a deliberate delay in alarm annunciation and
**must be disclosed as such**, not hidden.

**Silence and pause must be distinguishable.** A paused alarm resumes automatically
after a defined interval; a silenced alarm stays silent until a person acts. If the
nurse cannot tell these apart at a glance, a high-priority condition can be
effectively suppressed for an unbounded period. The nurse-station display therefore
distinguishes them by design.

## 4.5 Failure behaviour

| Failure | Required behaviour |
|---|---|
| Bedside network link lost | Local annunciation continues at the bedside. The hub marks the bed stale and shows the time of last contact. The station **must never display a frozen trace as live.** |
| Hub unavailable | Bedside units continue to alarm locally. This is the reason alarm evaluation is distributed. |
| Power interruption | Default alarm presets re-apply on restore. Essential supply takes the station and at least one bedside unit. |
| Time source unavailable | The hub flags alarm timelines as unsynchronised rather than presenting a plausible-looking but wrong ordering. |

**Default alarm presets must be re-applied** on power-up, on enabling the alarm
system, **on admitting a new patient**, and on restoring from total power loss. This
last point is the one most often missed in ward configuration: without it, a bed
adopted at a later date can inherit limits set for a different patient category, and
the alarm presets are locked to the responsible organisation so that an individual
operator cannot overwrite them.

## 4.6 Nurse station design

| Capability | Reference figure | 5-bed target |
|---|---|---|
| Patients per display | 16–36 on a 30-bed class system | **5–8, never more than 10** |
| Waveforms per patient | 8–12 | 5–6 |
| Full-disclosure waveform retention | 240 h | **≥ 72 h** |
| Trend retention | 240 h | **30 days** |
| Event recall | 3,000 events at 16 s either side | **≥ 500 events** |
| Measurements retained | 3,000 | **≥ 1,000** |

Host specification for a five-bed ward: a four-core processor, 8 GB of memory and a
250 GB solid-state store, against a 500 GB mechanical disk for the 64-bed class
system. One 1 kVA online UPS with at least 30 minutes of autonomy, and a RAID 1
mirrored host, because the hub is a single point of failure for the entire ward.

**Data backfill on reconnect.** When a bed rejoins after a network interruption, the
hub merges and de-duplicates the recovered interval rather than either dropping it or
presenting a discontinuous trace without indication. The redundancy model is
deliberate: UPS for power loss, RAID 1 for host loss, local bedside annunciation for
network loss.

## 4.7 Usability: the five-patient cognitive problem (IEC 62366-1)

A nurse watching five patients is the defining use-related hazard of this design, and
it is the strongest justification for including a usability standard in the project.

The hazard is **bed identity confusion**. An alarm must be attributable, within
seconds, to one of five patients whom the nurse may not currently be observing. Three
controls address it:

1. **Persistent, unambiguous bed identity** on every display tile, in every alarm
   presentation and in the printed record. The relational schema enforces that a bed
   has at most one open assignment, so the identity mapping itself cannot fork.
2. **Audible alarm differentiation by priority**, with distinct melodic structures
   rather than differing pitch alone — which is what the second amendment to the
   alarm standard introduced, having found that the original design gave eight
   high-priority alarms identical temporal structure.
3. **Alarm severity hierarchy across systems**, defined in section 7.4, so that a
   monitor alarm and a code blue do not compete as undifferentiated noise.

A summative evaluation would be required before release: five representative nurses
performing representative tasks against the specification, measuring whether they
correctly and promptly identify which patient an alarm belongs to.

## 4.8 Alarm fatigue and the suppression of nuisance alarms

Alarm fatigue is the leading cause of missed clinically significant alarms in
critical care. Three design responses are specified.

**Differentiate technical from physiological alarms.** A disconnected electrode is a
device fault, not a patient event, and must not be presented with the same urgency
as ventricular fibrillation. Both are represented in the schema — the `kind` field
distinguishes physiological, technical and system conditions — but they are ranked
and styled differently at the station.

**Manage known artefact sources.** NIBP-aware suppression of saturation alarms during
cuff inflation, with the delay disclosed per 4.4.1, is the standard example.

**Instrument nuisance rates rather than assert them.** The alarm standard **sets no
numeric nuisance-alarm budget**. Any figure quoted for this design is therefore a
**design target set by this project**, traceable to the alarm statistics function of
the central station, and not a figure inherited from a standard. The relational schema
supports the measurement: `escalation_count` on every alert, and a retained
acknowledgement record, together make alarm rates and response times computable per
bed, per parameter and per shift.

## 4.9 Alarm audio design

Two sound systems are specified, and keeping them separate is the point.

### 4.9.1 Why these sounds are synthesised rather than recorded

Real manufacturer alarm tones are **proprietary product intellectual property**.
No lawful source of a Dräger, Philips, GE, Mindray or Nihon Kohden alarm-tone
recording exists, and none was used.

That is not a compromise, and it is worth stating why. **IEC 60601-1-8 specifies
the alarm sounds parametrically** — fundamental frequency range, pulse duration,
the gap structure of the burst, and a tolerance on how closely the four largest
harmonics must sit together. It does not prescribe a waveform file. That is
deliberate: the requirement must be reproducible on a cheap piezo sounder as well
as on a mains-powered monitor. A faithful implementation driven from the
specification is therefore **more** accurate than any single manufacturer's
recording, which is merely one implementation of the same specification.

The timing parameters below are those of IEC 60601-1-8:2006+A1:2012 Tables 1 and
2, as reproduced in freely available manufacturer application literature.

### 4.9.2 The pulse tone

A two-part **lub-dup** pip on each detected heartbeat: a short "lub" at about
691 Hz followed by a "dub" at about 469 Hz. That interval is a perfect fifth and
sits very close to the true lub-dub of the heart, which is why it reads as a
heartbeat rather than as a beep. A single blip does not.

- **Rate** follows the pulse rate, one pip per detected beat.
- **Pitch** follows oxygen saturation, so a falling saturation is audible before
  the number is read.
- **Level** falls slightly with saturation as well.
- **Per-beat variation** of a few tenths of a percent is applied to pitch.
  Perfectly identical repeats read as synthetic; slight physiological variation
  reads as alive.

On real equipment **this tone comes from the bedside unit, not the central
station**, because five simultaneous pulse tones are unintelligible. The station
therefore makes the tone source **selectable per bed**, and the working prototype
implements exactly that.

**It is an information signal, not an alarm.** The standard classes the saturation
tone and the electrocardiogram waveform sound as information signals, and neither
may ever follow the alarm burst grammar.

### 4.9.3 The alarm signal

| Parameter | High | Medium | Low |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pulses per burst** | **10** | **3** | **2** |
| Pulse duration | 146 ms (range 75–200) | 200 ms (range 125–250) | 200 ms |
| Ordinary gap | 124 ms (range 50–125) | 124 ms | 124 ms |
| Special gap | 394 ms = 2×gap + duration, twice; plus 800 ms between the fifth and sixth (range 0.35–1.30 s) | — | — |
| Interburst interval | 5.0 s (range 2.5–15) | 9.0 s (range 2.5–30) | 18.0 s (over 15) |
| Relative level | 0 dB | −4 dB | −8 dB |

**The melody identifies the category; the pulse count identifies the priority.**
A real monitor does not emit one generic alarm, and that distinction is what lets
a nurse know the kind of problem before reading the screen.

| Category | Medium melody | High melody |
|---|---|---|
| **Cardiovascular** | c – e – g | c – e – g – g – C |
| **Oxygenation** | C – B – A | C – B – A – g – f |
| **Ventilation** | c – a – f | c – a – f – a – f |
| **Temperature** | c – d – e | c – d – e – e – C |
| **General** | c – c – c | c – c – c – c – c |

The cardiovascular melody **c – e – g** is the reserved figure in the standard, and
the high-priority form is that figure extended to five notes and played twice,
which is where the ten pulses come from.

Low priority is a single descending pair, e – c. Information signals receive one
short, soft, mid-register blip that is **deliberately not alarm-shaped**, because
an information signal is not an alarm condition.

### 4.9.4 Timbre — the parameter that decides whether it sounds clinical

This is the single most important choice, and it is where a naive synthesiser
fails. A pure sine, or an evenly-spaced 1-2-3-4 harmonic stack, sounds thin and
obviously synthetic.

Measured spectra of conforming alarm tones show a **flat harmonic stack**:
harmonics 1 and 3 through 9 sitting within about 5.5 dB of each other, with the
second partial some 26 dB down. That flatness is itself a requirement — the four
largest components must lie within 15 dB of each other — and the tolerance exists
so that direct and reflected sound in a ward cannot cancel one partial and leave
the alarm inaudible from some positions.

The design implements harmonics 1 through 9 with the second partial at −26 dB and
the remainder flat. **Measured on the working prototype: eleven harmonics present
between 300 and 4000 Hz against a requirement of four, and the four largest
components within 2.0 dB against a tolerance of 15 dB.**

Fundamentals sit between 260 and 700 Hz, below the 1000 Hz threshold recommended
for long-distance audibility. A 4.5 kHz low-pass emulates the roll-off of a small
piezo driver and removes the digital edge.

### 4.9.5 Relative level

The standard requires only that a high-priority burst be louder than medium,
which in turn is louder than low. The practical guidance is **three to six
decibels per step**; four is used here. The ladder is applied on **separate gain
buses**, so a lower priority can never exceed a higher one — that is normative,
so it is expressed as a constant rather than left to taste.

The pulse tone sits **18 dB below the high-priority bus**. It runs continuously,
and at parity it would mask every alarm. This figure is a design inference, not a
standard value: the standard does not specify the pulse tone level at all.

Absolute sound pressure is not deliverable from a browser — laptop speakers top
out well below the 70–80 dB(A) at one metre that a real monitor produces, against
a ward ambient of roughly 55 dB(A). **The relative dynamic ladder is what this
design specifies, and that is what makes the set legible.** A soft clipper and a
compressor stand in for the limiter that protects a real monitor's sounder.

### 4.9.6 Silence control

A **bounded pause** and an **indefinite silence** are separate states and are
presented differently, because conflating them allows a high-priority condition to
be suppressed for an unbounded period by a single press.

### 4.9.7 What is deliberately absent

The pulse repetition rates in pulses per minute from the standard's Table 3, the
absolute minimum sound pressure level, and the visual alarm parameters are **not
quoted**, because they sit inside a paywalled document and secondary sources were
found to misstate them — one published "compliance guide" conflates carrier
frequency with pulse repetition rate. The structures above are built from
parameters that were verified; the absolute rates are an implementation choice,
labelled as such rather than presented as compliance.

| Requirement | Where it is discharged |
|---|---|
| Audible priority differentiation | 4.9.3, and the category audition control in the prototype |
| Harmonic content and balance | 4.9.4, measured on the prototype |
| Information signals not routed as alarms | 4.9.2, enforced by a separate severity class and bus |
| Pause and silence distinguishable | 4.9.6 |
| Audible technical versus physiological | 4.8 |
| Alarm not dependent on the archival path | 4.2 |

<!-- source: report/05_data_model.md -->

The brief specifies six tables — Patients, Beds, Instruments, Vitals_Log, Alerts,
Staff — plus foreign keys, an index on `bed_id` with timestamp, constraints, and
an ER diagram. This section delivers those and explains four tables the brief does
not name but without which the design does not hold together.

The full executable schema is `db/01_schema.sql`; seed data is `db/02_seed.sql`.
The relationship view is `figures/m5_er_diagram.svg`.

## 5.1 Why PostgreSQL

Three requirements decide the engine, and none of them are generic "RDBMS"
requirements:

| Requirement | PostgreSQL feature |
|---|---|
| `Vitals_Log` will hold roughly 30 million rows per bed-week and must be aged out by policy | **Declarative range partitioning** — retention becomes `DROP TABLE` on a partition rather than a mass `DELETE` that bloats the heap and holds locks |
| A bed can never hold two overlapping patient assignments | **Exclusion constraints** — a declarative, index-backed guarantee |
| Alarm timelines across five beds and two stations must reconcile | Native **`TIMESTAMPTZ`** with real timezone semantics |

## 5.2 Entity relationships

```
Patient 1 ──< Admission 1 ──< Vitals_Log >── 1 Bed 1 ──< Instrument
                                        │            │            │
                                        │            │            └─ referenced by Vitals_Log
                                        │            │
                                        │            └──< Bed_Assignment >── 1 Admission
                                        │
                                        ├── 1 Alert ──< Alarm_Acknowledgement >── 1 Staff
                                        │
                                        └── 1 ABDM consent link

Staff 1 ──< Admission (admitting_staff_id)

Admission 1 ──< Consumable_Usage >── 1 Consumable
Admission 1 ──< Billing_Event
```

### 5.2.1 Four tables the brief does not list

Each is omitted from the brief but necessary, and each is a table the design
cannot be correct without.

**`admissions`.** A patient's stay spans days and may occupy several beds. Without
a first-class admission entity, `vitals_log` has no episode to belong to, discharge
has nothing to close, and ABDM care contexts have nothing to reference. This is the
Encounter in FHIR terms.

**`bed_assignments`.** A bed is occupied over a *time interval*, not permanently.
Collapsing this into `vitals_log.bed_id` makes it impossible to answer "who was in
bed 3 at 03:00 last night", and impossible to enforce that a bed holds one patient.

**`alarm_acknowledgements`.** IEC 60601-1-8 requires a **tamper-evident record of
alarm events** — a regulatory export obligation, not a query convenience. A single
`acknowledged_at` column on `alerts` records that *someone* responded but not who,
how many times, or whether the response was an acknowledgement, a silence or a
pause. Those are different clinical acts with different meanings.

**`sync_outbox`.** The mechanism for relational-to-MongoDB propagation. See 5.6.

Two integration tables complete the picture: `abdm_consent_links` and
`parameters`, the LOINC-terminology lookup.

## 5.3 Index design

The brief specifies an index on `bed_id` together with timestamp. Column **order**
is not incidental — the nurse-station access pattern is always *"one bed, newest
first"*, which is a range scan on `recorded_at` within an equality filter on
`bed_id`:

```sql
-- The primary time-series access path.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_vitals_bed_time
    ON vitals_log (bed_id, recorded_at DESC);

-- Per-parameter trend review across the whole ward.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_vitals_param_time
    ON vitals_log (parameter_code, recorded_at DESC);

-- The nurse-station alarm list: unacknowledged, most severe first.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ix_alerts_open
    ON alerts (acknowledged_at, priority, raised_at DESC);
```

## 5.4 Constraints that encode clinical safety

A schema that stores bad data correctly is not a passing schema. The constraints
below exist because each one corresponds to a specific way a monitoring system
can mislead a clinician.

| Constraint | Prevents |
|---|---|
| `ck_vitals_hr_plausible` | A 4000 bpm reading reaching a nurse's screen. This is a sensor or mapping fault, not a patient. |
| `ck_vitals_spo2_plausible` | Saturation above 100 %, which is not a physiological state |
| `ck_vitals_bp_plausible`, `ck_vitals_temp_plausible` | Out-of-range pressure and temperature |
| `ck_vitals_derived_provenance` | Mean arterial pressure recorded **without declaring what it was derived from**. MAP is computed as (SBP + 2·DBP)/3, never measured; a value without provenance is untraceable. |
| `ux_bed_assignments_open` | **Two patients mapped to one bed** — the single most dangerous data error in a ward system |
| `uq_vitals_source_row` | Duplicate rows from at-least-once broker redelivery |
| `ck_alerts_priority` | Alarm priorities outside the IEC 60601-1-8 Table 1 set |
| `ck_alerts_ack_by_staff` | An alarm acknowledged with no identified operator |
| `ck_vitals_clock_order` | A row arriving before the moment it describes |
| `ck_patients_abha_envelope` | An ABHA number reaching the database in plaintext |
| `ck_consent_status` | Consent states outside the ABDM value set |

### 5.4.1 Two clocks, deliberately

`vitals_log` carries both `recorded_at` — when the sensor sampled — and
`received_at` — when the hub durably wrote the row. The difference between them is
the network-transport component of the alarm latency budget that IEC 60601-1-8
requires to be disclosed. Collapsing them to one column makes the disclosure
impossible to produce.

### 5.4.2 Provisional versus final

IHE PCD-XR solves push-message reliability with a two-phase commit: the sender
delivers a provisional report, the receiver acknowledges it as provisional, and
only when the complete data set has arrived does a second message make it final.
The receiver therefore never silently treats half a panel as complete.

That maps directly onto the FHIR R4 observation lifecycle, which already defines
`preliminary` and `final`:

> A blood-pressure panel is written as three `preliminary` rows. When the third
> arrives, all three are promoted to `final`. A trend query filters on
> `record_status = 'final'`, so a partially delivered panel is never charted.

### 5.4.3 A defect the build harness caught

Enforcing `received_at >= recorded_at` initially failed on seed data written as
`09:00:00Z` against `09:00:00.120Z`. The cause is genuine and worth recording:
**ISO-8601 timestamps with variable fractional-second precision do not sort
correctly as strings**, because `.` (0x2E) orders below `Z` (0x5A). PostgreSQL
compares `TIMESTAMPTZ` natively and is immune, but any system that serialises to
text — including an MQTT payload or an ABDM JSON body — must normalise to fixed
fractional width before it can be range-sorted or compared.

## 5.5 Executable verification

The schema is not merely printed in this report; it is executed. The build harness
loads it, loads seed data, then attempts to insert deliberately invalid rows and
asserts that each is **rejected for the reason claimed**.

```sql
-- The nurse-station alarm list. Unacknowledged only, most severe first.
SELECT a.priority, b.bed_label, a.parameter_code, a.message, a.raised_at
  FROM alerts a
  JOIN beds b ON b.id = a.bed_id
 WHERE a.acknowledged_at IS NULL
 ORDER BY a.priority, a.raised_at DESC;
```

```sql
-- Bed occupancy, including unoccupied and out-of-service beds.
SELECT b.bed_label, b.operational_status, p.mrn, ba.assigned_at
  FROM beds b
  LEFT JOIN bed_assignments ba ON ba.bed_id = b.id AND ba.released_at IS NULL
  LEFT JOIN admissions a ON a.id = ba.admission_id
  LEFT JOIN patients p ON p.id = a.patient_id
 ORDER BY b.bed_label;
```

```sql
-- Provenance audit for every computed mean arterial pressure.
SELECT id, value_num, derived_from, recorded_at
  FROM vitals_log
 WHERE parameter_code = '8478-0'
 ORDER BY recorded_at DESC;
```

```sql
-- Consumables at or below reorder level, worst first.
SELECT sku, description, on_hand, reorder_level, unit_cost_inr
  FROM consumables
 WHERE on_hand <= reorder_level
 ORDER BY (reorder_level - on_hand) DESC;
```

The harness applies ten behavioural assertions, including a **positive control**
that a correctly-formed, properly-provenanced MAP row *is* accepted. Without that
control the nine rejection tests would still report success if every statement
errored out for an unrelated reason — which is precisely the failure mode this
harness encountered and had to be corrected for.

## 5.6 Relational to document-store propagation

Milestone G3 requires a MongoDB-backed record sync. The design principle is:

> **The RDBMS is the system of record. MongoDB is a read model for aggregation.
> Neither is written by the application in parallel.**

A dual write has no atomicity across two stores, so the databases are guaranteed
to drift, and the drift is silent. The harness cannot test what is not specified,
so this is stated as a design decision rather than an implementation.

**Change data capture via a transactional outbox**, rather than log-based CDC, is
selected for this project: it is simple, transactional, and at-least-once, and it
does not require the application to enable binary logging.

```sql
-- Publisher side: reads unpublished outbox rows, marks them, streams to Mongo.
SELECT id, source_table, source_pk, operation, payload, is_tombstone
  FROM sync_outbox
 WHERE published_at IS NULL
 ORDER BY id
 LIMIT 500;
```

| Option | Latency | Intrusive | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Log-based CDC (Debezium on the write-ahead log) | ms–s | No | Preferred at production scale |
| **Transactional outbox** | ms | No (one extra table) | **Selected** — simplest correct option |
| Trigger-based | s | Yes, degrades writes | Avoid |
| Periodic polling on a watermark | min–hr | No | Fallback; misses deletes |
| Dual write from application code | real | — | **Rejected** — no atomicity, guaranteed drift |

### 5.6.1 Non-negotiable properties of the consumer

1. **Idempotent upserts** keyed on the source primary key — CDC is at-least-once.
2. **Tombstones.** CDC delivers deletes; replaying one must not resurrect a row.
   Enforced by `is_tombstone` and `ck_outbox_tombstone`.
3. **Schema-evolution tolerance** — added and removed columns must not crash the
   consumer.
4. **Never mirror Aadhaar, OTP or password into MongoDB.** Exclusion belongs at
   the transformer, not at the reader, or it will eventually be missed.
5. **Honour `data_erase_at` in both stores.** A consent erasure that clears only
   the relational store has not happened.

## 5.7 Volume and retention

At 5 beds × 10 parameters × 1 reading/second, `vitals_log` grows by roughly
**30 million rows per bed-week**. Three consequences follow:

1. **Partition monthly** on `recorded_at`, so retention is `DROP TABLE`.
2. **Waveform data does not belong in `vitals_log` rows.** Full-disclosure
   waveforms should live in a time-series or object store keyed by bed, start
   time and duration. The reference implementation for this class of system keeps
   240 hours of full disclosure and 3,000 events at 16 seconds of waveform either
   side of each alarm.
3. **Trend queries must be bounded.** Unbounded scans of a partitioned table
   spanning five beds will fall off the index and become the dominant load on the
   hub. Section 4.6 sets the retention target: 72 hours of full disclosure and
   30 days of trends.
