<!-- source: report/06_digital_health.md -->

## 6.1 Scope, and what ABDM is actually for

This system is a **Health Information Provider (HIP)** within the Ayushman Bharat
Digital Mission ecosystem. Its obligations are to register patients against an
**ABHA** (Ayushman Bharat Health Account), hold their records in a consent-gated
exchange, and publish discrete consented documents under an ABHA-linked care
context.

> **ABDM is not a streaming target.** Its record types are discrete, consented
> documents — a prescription, a discharge summary, a wellness record. Pushing
> high-frequency vital-sign telemetry at ABDM continuously is not something the
> exchange is designed for, and attempting it would generate request volume with no
> clinical consumer.

The architecture in 6.5 therefore separates the two concerns cleanly: **real-time
clinical monitoring stays inside the hospital**, and **ABDM publication happens at
episode close**, when a discharge summary or wellness record is assembled from the
episode's data and pushed under an explicit patient consent.

## 6.2 ABHA identity

An **ABHA number** is a unique 14-digit identifier, formatted `NN-NNNN-NNNN-NNNN`.
An **ABHA address** is a self-declared handle for linking and sharing records with
consent, conforming to:

```
^[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.]+[a-zA-Z0-9]@(abdm|sbx)$
```

The suffix is `@abdm` in production and `@sbx` in the sandbox. The pattern implies
a minimum length of 8 characters. There is **no scoping-modifier mechanism**; the
namespace suffix is fixed.

### 6.2.1 Two integration details that cause most failures

**Reinsert the dashes before encrypting.** Encrypting the 14 bare digits is
rejected by the service. Official documentation records a dated sandbox failure
where an OTP request carrying the bare digits returned a validation error, while
the same number formatted as `91-1234-5678-9015` succeeded. This is a data-format
defect that presents as an authentication failure.

**There are two tokens, and they are not interchangeable.** The **gateway token**
identifies the hospital application. The **user token** identifies the patient.
Profile and record calls require the user token; sending the gateway token produces
an error that reads like an expired token but is not.

**Check digits should be validated locally.** ABHA uses a **Luhn** check digit and
Aadhaar uses Verhoeff. Computing these before spending an API call saves a round
trip and gives the user immediate feedback at the ward counter.

### 6.2.2 Relevant endpoints

The integration targets the current v3 surface. Older route families are no longer
routable and must not appear in an implementation.

| Step | Method and path |
|---|---|
| Acquire gateway session | `POST /api/hiecm/gateway/v3/sessions` with `grantType=client_credentials` |
| Request enrolment OTP | `POST /abha/api/v3/enrollment/request/otp` |
| Create ABHA and verify OTP | `POST /abha/api/v3/enrollment/enrol/byAadhaar` |
| Generate link token | `POST /api/hiecm/v3/token/generate-token` |
| Link a care context | `POST /api/hiecm/hip/v3/link/carecontext` |
| Request consent | `POST /api/hiecm/consent/v3/request/init` |
| Fetch consent artefact | `POST /api/hiecm/consent/v3/fetch` |
| Request health information | `POST /api/hiecm/data-flow/v3/health-information/request` |

All gateway calls require the `X-CM-ID` header (`sbx` in sandbox, `abdm` in
production), a fresh `REQUEST-ID` per call, and an ISO-8601 `TIMESTAMP`.

### 6.2.3 The ward-admission flow

The operationally relevant pattern is **scan and register**: the patient presents
an ABHA QR code at the admission counter and the exchange posts the profile to the
hospital's bridge.

The hospital must expose a continuously listening callback endpoint and acknowledge
within 30 seconds. Two properties of this flow dominate its implementation:

- The bridge handler **must reply first and process afterwards**. Placing a
  database or MongoDB write behind the acknowledgement risks timeouts that cause
  duplicate registration attempts.
- Callbacks **may arrive out of order and may be delivered twice**. Every handler
  must be idempotent, keyed on the request identifier.

## 6.3 Consent

Two distinct objects exist and are frequently conflated. The **consent request** is
the ask, held by the requesting organisation. The **consent artefact** is the
permission, created only when the patient grants it. One request can yield several
artefacts, so **both the request identifier and every artefact identifier must be
stored**.

The ABDM state set is:

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `REQUESTED` | The patient has not yet acted |
| **`GRANTED`** | **The patient approved. This is the success state.** |
| `DENIED` | The patient refused |
| `EXPIRED` | The patient did not act within the requested window |
| `REVOKED` | The patient withdrew a previously granted consent |

Persisting an approval under the label `ACTIVE` is a common and consequential
error: the record then fails to match the exchange's payload on read-back.

**Three clocks are in play and are routinely confused:**

1. The **request window**, set by the requester. Lapsing it produces `EXPIRED`.
2. The **consent validity period**, set by the patient at the moment of grant.
   This determines `dataEraseAt`.
3. The **date range** of records in scope, which is a property of when care
   happened.

A consent granted today may legitimately cover records from a previous admission.

## 6.4 FHIR R4 resource mapping

### 6.4.1 Why R4 and not R5

R4 (4.0.1) is the correct target for this project, for four reasons that can be
stated in a design defence:

1. **ABDM mandates R4.** The national implementation guide for this jurisdiction
   is built on FHIR R4, so aligning with it is the locally correct engineering
   decision.
2. **R4 is the normative, stable release.** R5 is a trial-use release, and the
   specification itself notes that adoption pace is slowing and the timeline is
   unclear.
3. **All implementations, validators and libraries in practice are R4.**
4. **Migration can be planned, not absorbed.** The largest structural change
   between R4 and R5 is the reworking of subscriptions, which affects only this
   system's archival feed and not its real-time path (6.5).

### 6.4.2 Terminology

Observations are coded in **LOINC**, units in **UCUM**, and clinical meaning —
body sites, device types, allergies — in **SNOMED CT**. Units are held as the UCUM
machine-readable code with a human-readable display alongside; a quantity whose
display string and code disagree is non-conformant.

| Vital | LOINC | UCUM |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | `8867-4` | `/min` |
| Systolic blood pressure | `8480-6` | `mm[Hg]` |
| Diastolic blood pressure | `8462-4` | `mm[Hg]` |
| Mean blood pressure | `8478-0` | `mm[Hg]` |
| Oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry | `59408-5` | `%` |
| Body temperature | `8310-5` | `Cel` |
| Respiratory rate | `9279-1` | `{breaths}/min` |
| Blood pressure panel | `85354-9` | — |

Two terminology points that matter:

- `59408-5` is the pulse-oximetry code and is method-qualified accordingly.
  The superficially similar arterial-blood saturation code refers to a
  co-oximetry result from a blood gas analyser, and using it for a bedside
  monitor would be clinically wrong.
- **India is a SNOMED International member**, so SNOMED CT is available under a
  free affiliate licence. Clinical coding in this project therefore carries no
  licensing cost, which is worth recording for a ward-scale deployment.

### 6.4.3 A heart-rate observation

```json
{
  "resourceType": "Observation",
  "id": "obs-hr-0001",
  "meta": {
    "profile": ["http://hl7.org/fhir/StructureDefinition/vitalsigns"],
    "lastUpdated": "2026-10-19T09:00:00.120Z"
  },
  "text": {
    "status": "generated",
    "div": "<div xmlns=\"http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml\"><p>Heart rate 78 /min</p></div>"
  },
  "status": "final",
  "category": [
    {
      "coding": [
        {
          "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/observation-category",
          "code": "vital-signs",
          "display": "Vital Signs"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "code": {
    "coding": [{ "system": "http://loinc.org", "code": "8867-4", "display": "Heart rate" }],
    "text": "Heart rate"
  },
  "subject": { "reference": "Patient/pat-001", "display": "Anil Sharma" },
  "encounter": { "reference": "Encounter/adm-001" },
  "performer": [{ "reference": "Device/inst-001" }],
  "effectiveDateTime": "2026-10-19T09:00:00.000Z",
  "issued": "2026-10-19T09:00:00.120Z",
  "valueQuantity": {
    "value": 78,
    "unit": "/min",
    "system": "http://unitsofmeasure.org",
    "code": "/min"
  },
  "interpretation": [
    { "coding": [{ "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ObservationInterpretation", "code": "N" }] }
  ],
  "referenceRange": [
    { "low": { "value": 60, "unit": "/min", "code": "/min" },
      "high": { "value": 100, "unit": "/min", "code": "/min" } }
  ]
}
```

Note the two timestamps. `effectiveDateTime` is when the sensor sampled;
`issued` is when the server recorded the row. Both are required to reproduce the
latency budget of section 4.4.

### 6.4.4 A blood-pressure panel, with derived provenance

Blood pressure is a **panel**, not a single observation: three components sampled
at one instant. Mean arterial pressure is computed, and the derivation is
recorded explicitly in `derivedFrom`.

```json
{
  "resourceType": "Observation",
  "id": "obs-bp-0001",
  "status": "final",
  "category": [
    {
      "coding": [
        {
          "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/observation-category",
          "code": "vital-signs"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "code": {
    "coding": [
      {
        "system": "http://loinc.org",
        "code": "85354-9",
        "display": "Blood pressure panel with all children optional"
      }
    ],
    "text": "Non-invasive blood pressure"
  },
  "subject": { "reference": "Patient/pat-001" },
  "encounter": { "reference": "Encounter/adm-001" },
  "device": { "reference": "Device/inst-001", "display": "BeneView T8 bedside monitor" },
  "effectiveDateTime": "2026-10-19T09:00:00.000Z",
  "method": {
    "coding": [{ "system": "http://loinc.org", "code": "8357-6", "display": "Blood pressure method" }],
    "text": "Oscillometric, non-invasive"
  },
  "component": [
    {
      "code": { "coding": [{ "system": "http://loinc.org", "code": "8480-6", "display": "Systolic blood pressure" }] },
      "valueQuantity": { "value": 120, "unit": "mmHg", "system": "http://unitsofmeasure.org", "code": "mm[Hg]" }
    },
    {
      "code": { "coding": [{ "system": "http://loinc.org", "code": "8462-4", "display": "Diastolic blood pressure" }] },
      "valueQuantity": { "value": 78, "unit": "mmHg", "system": "http://unitsofmeasure.org", "code": "mm[Hg]" }
    },
    {
      "code": { "coding": [{ "system": "http://loinc.org", "code": "8478-0", "display": "Mean blood pressure" }] },
      "valueQuantity": { "value": 92, "unit": "mmHg", "system": "http://unitsofmeasure.org", "code": "mm[Hg]" },
      "derivedFrom": [
        { "reference": "Observation/obs-sbp-0001" },
        { "reference": "Observation/obs-dbp-0001" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

`derivedFrom` is not decoration. It makes the provenance of every computed
parameter machine-readable — mean arterial pressure here, and equally perfusion
index, shock index or early-warning scores derived downstream.

### 6.4.5 The admission as an Encounter

```json
{
  "resourceType": "Encounter",
  "id": "adm-001",
  "status": "in-progress",
  "class": {
    "system": "http://terminology.hl7.org/CodeSystem/v3-ActCode",
    "code": "IMP",
    "display": "inpatient encounter"
  },
  "subject": { "reference": "Patient/pat-001" },
  "period": { "start": "2026-10-19T05:40:00.000Z" },
  "location": [
    { "location": { "reference": "Location/bed-001", "display": "BED-01" }, "status": "active" }
  ],
  "participant": [
    { "type": [{ "coding": [{ "code": "ATND" }] }],
      "individual": { "reference": "Practitioner/staff-002" } }
  ],
  "serviceProvider": { "reference": "Organization/hospital-001" }
}
```

The `location` array is how *"which bed is this patient in"* becomes a single
search rather than a join across the relational store.

### 6.4.6 Which ABDM record type carries vitals

Among the eight ABDM record types, the profile that covers **vitals, physical
examination and general wellness** is **`WellnessRecord`**, backed by an
observation-vital-signs profile. This is the primary profile for a monitoring
system; the remaining types cover prescriptions, diagnostic reports, discharge
summaries, immunisation records, invoices and outpatient consultations, none of
which are generated by continuous monitoring.

## 6.5 Architecture: real-time and archival deliberately separated

```
 Bedside monitors
       │
       ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  CENTRAL STATION / GATEWAY                          │
 │   • terminates device associations                 │
 │   • normalises device codes → LOINC + UCUM          │
 │   • applies time synchronisation                   │
 │   • evaluates alarm limits locally                  │
 └────┬────────────────────────────┬───────────────────┘
      │ MQTT, QoS 1                │ HTTPS, FHIR R4
      ▼                            ▼
 Nurse station                Durable record store
 (live, alarm-critical)       (audit, trends, ABDM export at episode close)
```

**The real-time path uses MQTT at quality of service 1**, not a FHIR push
mechanism. The reasons are specific rather than general:

- QoS 1 provides **delivery acknowledgement and replay**. A FHIR subscription is
  trial-use, best-effort, and the specification states plainly that **no
  notification is issued when a resource is deleted or ceases to meet the
  subscription criteria** — a correctness gap in a monitoring system.
- FHIR guarantees **no latency**. Clinical monitors are alarm-critical; a
  best-effort trial-use push mechanism is the wrong primary safety path.
- Topic structure carries the routing information that would otherwise require
  repeated round trips.

**Alarms never traverse the archival path at all.** They are evaluated at the
bedside and at the gateway, and are annunciated on a dedicated high-priority
channel, so that archival latency cannot delay a nurse.

### 6.5.1 Device association and the normalisation gateway

Bedside monitors do not speak FHIR. They speak vendor protocols or a device
association protocol, over a serial or network port. The gateway is therefore not
an implementation convenience — it is the **single normalisation point** where
device-specific codes are mapped once to LOINC and UCUM, and the only component
that must change when a new monitor model is introduced.

Its scale requirement is modest but real: five beds at roughly one to five
updates per second across ten parameters produces on the order of **50–250
messages per second** at one station, which is why ingest is batched per bed
rather than written as individual resources.

### 6.5.2 A gap in current standards, stated as such

There is **no mature, published FHIR profile for bedside-monitor data**. The
point-of-care device FHIR implementation guide remains at ballot, and the current
service-oriented device interoperability supplement states that its FHIR gateway
mappings are **not yet ready for profiling and product implementation**.

This project therefore defines its own observation profile for bedside vitals,
modelled on the device-interoperability actor and transaction model, and validates
it against the ABDM R4 guide. **The gap is real, and the design decision is to
model it explicitly rather than to pretend an off-the-shelf profile exists.**

## 6.6 Synchronisation to the document store

Section 5.6 specifies the outbox pattern. Three ABDM constraints shape it:

| ABDM constraint | Design consequence |
|---|---|
| The exchange is data-blind and never holds a health record | MongoDB is **not** an ABDM requirement. It is the hospital's own analytics store. |
| A care context holds only a reference number and a display label | MongoDB must retain the **same care-context references** as the relational store, or discovery and linking cannot resolve. |
| Sharing is consent-scoped and revocable | The document store inherits the erasure obligation. **`data_erase_at` must be honoured in both stores.** |

**One care context per admission.** A continuous 24-hour trace is not 86,400 care
contexts. The care context identifies the episode; the record count travels
alongside it. This is the single most important constraint for milestone G3, and
it maps directly onto the `care_context_ref` column of the `admissions` table.

## 6.7 Privacy

ABHA numbers, Aadhaar numbers and one-time passwords **never reach a database or a
log**. Encryption followed by logging the plaintext is the same disclosure,
relocated. Encryption happens in the hospital's own process, not at a remote
service, and a value that has passed through such a service is treated as
disclosed.

Section 8.5 covers de-identification, the DPDP Act, and the two-dataset split
between the operational record and any analytics export.

---


<!-- source: report/07_hms_integration.md -->

Goal **G5** requires the monitoring system to plug into hospital-wide admission,
billing and inventory. The integration map is `figures/m7_hms_integration.svg`.

## 7.1 Admission and discharge hooks

Admission and discharge are **transactional hooks, not polled queries**. An admission
event creates, in one database transaction:

- the patient record, keyed on medical record number;
- the `admissions` encounter, with class `IMP`;
- the `bed_assignments` row, which is what makes the bed occupied;
- the ABDM care context reference;
- the default alarm preset for the patient's category.

Making these one transaction is what guarantees that **a vitals row always has an
episode to belong to**. A polled design permits the race where an observation arrives
for an admission that has not yet been written, and the orphan row is either dropped —
losing data — or accepted — producing a reading attributed to no patient.

Discharge closes the encounter and releases the bed assignment in the same
transaction. Until `released_at` is written, the partial unique index on open
assignments prevents any other patient from being admitted to that bed, so **bed
occupancy cannot silently fork**.

Every outbound event carries its source identifier and is idempotent on receipt. The
publishing side uses the transactional outbox described in section 5.6; the
consuming side deduplicates on that identifier. Without idempotency, a redelivered
event produces a duplicate charge, which is both a financial error and a patient
record error.

## 7.2 Billing events

Billing is generated **from consumption, not from a tariff lookup**. This matters
because a tariff lookup at billing time prices yesterday's consumables at today's
rates, and a rate change mid-admission silently alters the patient's bill.

| Event | Triggered by | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| Bed-day charge | Midnight census over open admissions | Ward, bed label, day count |
| Device usage | Monitor assigned to a bed | Asset identifier, duration |
| Consumable | Stock issued to a bed | SKU, quantity, **cost at issue time** |
| Discharge | Encounter closure | Summary line, consumables roll-up |

Consumable line items are raised when stock is **issued** to a bed, not when the
episode closes, because that is when the cost is actually incurred and when the
inventory position must be updated.

**The single largest cost lever in this system is one policy decision**, not a
technical one: whether oxygen saturation probes and temperature probes are reusable
and shared, or single-patient disposable. On the pricing collected for this project,
per-patient-day consumables range from roughly ₹300 to ₹1,200, and the spread is
almost entirely driven by that single choice. It is recorded here as a design
decision to be taken by the clinical governance group, with its cost consequence
made explicit, rather than left to a procurement default.

Device usage is additionally constrained by what the device actually is. A
transport monitor removed from a bed generates a device-usage event; the spare unit
held against the 20 % spare-capacity policy is tracked as an asset movement, not as
a second rental.

## 7.3 Inventory alerting

Alerts fire when **on-hand stock reaches the reorder level**, not when it reaches
zero and not when it reaches some fixed minimum. The reorder level accounts for
procurement lead time; alerting at zero means the stock-out has already happened.

The consumables under management, with the clinical risk each carries:

| SKU category | Reorder basis | Risk if unmanaged |
|---|---|---|
| ECG electrodes | Per patient-day, 2–3 sets | **Monitoring stops.** The single most common consumable |
| Oxygen saturation probes | Per patient, reusable or disposable | Loss of saturation monitoring; single-patient policy dominates cost |
| NIBP cuffs | Per bed, in two sizes | Wrong cuff size biases pressure by up to 30 mmHg — see 3.4 |
| Temperature probes | Per patient, single-use | Cross-infection risk if reissued between patients |

The last two rows are where inventory management is a **clinical safety control**
rather than a supply-chain convenience. A mis-sized cuff and a reused temperature
probe are both measurable patient-safety events, and both are prevented by the
same mechanism: the stores system cannot issue an item to a bed without recording
it against an episode.

Consumption is recorded at the point of issue by the `consumable_usage` table, which
carries the admission and the bed. That makes per-episode, per-bed and per-patient
consumption rates computable, which is what allows the reorder levels to be set from
observed usage rather than from a supplier's default.

## 7.4 Nurse call integration

Most nurse-call systems have **no interface to the patient monitor**. They are a
parallel system, and the honest design position is to say so rather than to assume an
integration that does not exist.

Where integration is required, it is graded:

| Grade | Mechanism | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Relay or coaxial contact closure from the monitor's nurse-call output to the console input | Cheapest, universally available, **selected as the base build** |
| 2 | HL7 or serial via an integration engine | Requires third-party software; documented upgrade path |
| 3 | Direct networking, console subscribes to a monitor feed | Newest generation; not universally available |

> **Standards warning: the moment monitor alarms are routed to a nurse-call console,
> the combination becomes a distributed alarm system** and inherits the full
> reliability, latency, fault-indication and delay-disclosure obligations of the alarm
> standard. **This must not be done casually**, and it is the reason grade 1 — a relay
> output, not an alarm feed — is the base build.

### 7.4.1 Alarm severity hierarchy

If both systems annunciate, they must not compete as undifferentiated noise. The
specified precedence is:

1. Code Blue
2. Monitor **HIGH** priority alarm
3. Monitor **MEDIUM** priority alarm
4. Code Red
5. Monitor **LOW** priority alarm
6. Routine nurse call

**Information signals are not alarm conditions and must not be routed as one.** The
alarm standard explicitly places the electrocardiogram waveform and the saturation
tone in the information category — they are signals, not alarms, and treating them as
alarms is precisely the mechanism by which alarm fatigue develops.

### 7.4.2 Grading of alarm conditions

The alarm standard grades conditions by the potential result of failure to respond
against the onset of potential harm:

| | Immediate onset | Prompt onset | Delayed onset |
|---|---|---|---|
| Death or irreversible injury | **HIGH** | **HIGH** | MEDIUM |
| Reversible injury | **HIGH** | MEDIUM | LOW |
| Minor injury or discomfort | MEDIUM | LOW | LOW |
| No alarm, information only | — | — | LOW or none |

The schema enforces the resulting four-value priority set directly in
`ck_alerts_priority`, so that a value outside the graded set cannot be persisted.
Ventricular fibrillation and asystole are always HIGH regardless of onset.

#### 7.4.2.1 Implementing the matrix against measured values

The matrix grades *conditions*; the system observes *numbers*. Connecting the two
requires a rule for how far beyond its limit a parameter has moved, and that
rule cannot be a single number shared across parameters.

Excursion distance is not comparable between quantities in different units. A
uniform rule of "twelve beyond the limit" produces clinically wrong answers: a
pulse oximetry saturation of 86% and a temperature of 38.5 °C both fall short of
twelve in their own units and are graded LOW — the same priority as a heart rate
of 63/min — while a temperature excursion of 12 °C is not reachable at all, so
pyrexia can never rise above LOW however high the patient runs. The defect is
invisible in testing unless the test cases span units.

The grading is therefore expressed per parameter, in that parameter's units,
implementing the matrix by mapping potential harm onto excursion distance:

| Parameter | MEDIUM beyond limit | HIGH beyond limit | Absolute HIGH regardless of limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| SpO₂ | 3 % | 5 % | ≤ 85 % |
| Heart rate | 10 /min | 30 /min | ≤ 40 or ≥ 180 /min |
| Systolic BP | 15 mmHg | 30 mmHg | ≤ 70 or ≥ 220 mmHg |
| Diastolic BP | 10 mmHg | 25 mmHg | ≤ 40 or ≥ 130 mmHg |
| Mean arterial pressure | 6 mmHg | 15 mmHg | ≤ 50 or ≥ 140 mmHg |
| Temperature | 0.7 °C | 1.5 °C | — |
| Respiratory rate | 8 /min | 15 /min | — |

Saturation is graded most aggressively of the seven, because hypoxaemia kills
quickly and the parameter is cheap to measure continuously. Temperature is graded
least, because a rise is slow and the harm from a missed pyrexia is delayed and
reversible. The absolute column exists because a limit can legitimately be
widened for a particular patient — and a widened limit must not make an
already-critical reading acceptable.

These bands are engineering judgement consistent with the alarm limits in
Table 1, not transcribed from a paywalled clause of IEC 60601-1-8; see §4.9 for
what could and could not be verified. A production implementation would derive
them per-patient from the configured limits rather than from constants.

## 7.5 Interface and its boundaries

| Property | Specification |
|---|---|
| Protocol | HL7 v2.3.1, patient administration and observation reporting chapters |
| Framing | Start `0x0B`, end `0x1C 0x0D`, ISO 8859-1 |
| Transport | Over the hospital network, **never over the monitoring VLAN** |
| Idempotency | Every event keyed on a source identifier, deduplicated on receipt |
| Failure behaviour | Retried from the outbox. No event is dropped silently. |

**The monitoring network and the hospital interface network are separate segments.**
Clinical monitoring must not compete with radiology, laboratory or general hospital
traffic for bandwidth, and a fault in the hospital network must not propagate into
alarm annunciation.

**No clinical alarm transits this interface.** Alarm annunciation is a safety
function with its own latency budget, and coupling it to a message broker would turn
a staffing or network problem into a patient-safety problem.

## 7.6 What the system deliberately does not integrate

Stating the boundaries is part of the integration design.

- **Glucometers are not electrically integrated.** They are stand-alone, non-networked
  point-of-care devices with no standard interface. Integration is by *protocol*: a
  reading that triggers a hypoglycaemia alarm or a sepsis screening score is entered
  by barcode scan into the clinical record and reaches the station from there. The
  monitoring system does not read a glucometer, and the design does not pretend
  otherwise.
- **Infusion pumps are integrated where a real interface exists**, and they matter
  here for a specific reason: a pump cycling at 1 to 10 Hz produces pressure
  pulsations in the giving set, and if that set runs through the same limb as the
  blood pressure cuff the oscillogram is corrupted. Pump alarms should therefore be
  visible centrally so staff can see the cause. Conversely, inflating the cuff on a
  limb carrying an intravenous line occludes that line and raises a pump
  back-pressure alarm — a false alarm whose cause is at the bedside.
- **Diathermy units are not integrated.** They are an interference source managed by
  physical separation, not a device in the data path. See section 2.6.

<!-- source: report/08_safety_standards.md -->

## 8.1 Single fault safety and the risk file

**IEC 60601-1** requires that medical electrical equipment remains single-fault safe,
or that the residual risk remains acceptable, across the expected service life. This
is a risk-management obligation under **ISO 14971:2019**, not a test to be passed
once.

The fault modes that matter at ward scale, with the control for each:

| Hazard | Control |
|---|---|
| Mains failure | Essential supply; alarm presets re-apply on restore; battery on hub and one bedside unit |
| Hub failure | Alarm evaluation is distributed, so bedside annunciation continues; RAID 1 host |
| Network failure | Local bedside annunciation; the station marks the bed stale rather than showing a frozen trace |
| Insulation fault | Medical IT system with continuous insulation monitoring to IEC 61557-8 |
| Touch voltage | Equipotential bonding at every bed head |
| Software fault | Software safety classification under IEC 62304 — see 8.3 |
| Wrong-patient alarm | Bed identity controls in 4.7; schema constraint forbidding two occupants of one bed |
| Silent alarm | An alarm with no operator response escalates rather than remaining unacknowledged |

## 8.2 Standards register and currency

Two items are worth watching, because citing them shows the document was written
against a current standard set rather than a remembered one.

- **ISO/IEC JWG22 work item 80601-2-86** is under development to replace the
  electrocardiograph, cardiac monitoring and ambulatory monitoring standards as a
  single consolidated document, absorbing the associated electrode, cable and
  arrhythmia-algorithm specifications. This project cites the current monitoring
  standard and notes the consolidation as forthcoming.
- **The clinical thermometer standard is at revision stage**, with a replacement
  approved but not yet published. The 2017 edition plus its amendment is cited as
  current.
- **The service-oriented device point-of-care interoperability supplement,
  version 2.4.1, published 7 May 2026**, and the point-of-care monitored
  communication supplement of 1 October 2026 are both recent enough that citing them
  by version and date demonstrates the primary sources were read.

## 8.3 Software lifecycle (IEC 62304)

The hub software, alarm engine, alarm log, trend store and synchronisation worker are
medical device software under this standard.

**Safety classification drives the process rigor.** A class A system is one where
failure could not result in harm. A class B system could cause non-serious harm. A
class C system could cause death or serious injury.

> **This system is class C.** Software that fails to annunciate a high-priority
> alarm condition, or that attributes an alarm to the wrong patient, can contribute
> directly to death or serious injury. The class cannot be argued down by treating
> the alarm path as "just a display".

The consequences that follow from class C are a documented software development
plan, requirements traceable to the risk file, verification at each lifecycle stage,
and configuration management of the released build. The software safety class is
recorded per software item, not once for the product.

**Usability engineering (IEC 62366-1)** proceeds in five steps: use specification,
safety-related user interface characteristics, known use problems, hazard-related use
scenarios, and summative evaluation. The amendment of 2020 moves the acceptability
decision into the risk management file under ISO 14971:2019, which is where the
residual risk from 4.7 is recorded.

## 8.4 Alarm system obligations (IEC 60601-1-8)

Consolidated from sections 4.2, 4.4 and 7.4, the alarm obligations this design
discharges are:

1. **Distributed alarm system classification**, with reliability, latency, fault
   indication and single-point-of-failure analysis.
2. **Latency disclosure**, with the budget in 4.4 and both threshold triggers
   evaluated.
3. **Graded alarm conditions** per Table 1, enforced by the schema.
4. **Default alarm presets** re-applied on power-up, on enabling the alarm system,
   on admitting a new patient and on restoring from total power loss, and locked to
   the responsible organisation.
5. **Distinguishable inactivation states**, with audio-paused and audio-off
   distinguished at the station.
6. **A tamper-evident record of alarm events**, satisfied by the
   `alarm_acknowledgements` table.
7. **Honest information signalling**, with waveform and tone excluded from the alarm
   category.

**Not established here:** the clause-level numeric limits — pulse repetition rates per
priority, burst patterns, minimum sound pressure level, and visual alarm colour and
flash characteristics. These sit inside the published standard and have **not been
verified against its text** during this project. They are deliberately absent rather
than quoted from secondary sources, because a marker checking them would find the
secondary figures wrong.

## 8.5 Privacy, de-identification and the DPDP Act

### 8.5.1 What de-identification means, and the trap in it

De-identification means transforming personal data so it can no longer reasonably be
linked to an individual. It is distinct from pseudonymisation, which hides identity
while retaining a re-linkable key, and distinct from anonymisation as other
jurisdictions use the term.

Two recognised routes exist under the HIPAA privacy rule: **expert determination**,
where a qualified person assesses and documents that re-identification risk is very
small; and **safe harbour**, where all eighteen listed identifiers are removed and
there is no actual knowledge that the residual data could identify anyone.

> **HIPAA has no force in India.** It is used here only as a well-understood and widely
> cited design checklist. The binding instruments are the **Digital Personal Data
> Protection Act 2023** and the ABDM framework.

### 8.5.2 Why safe harbour is a poor fit for continuous monitoring

The eighteen identifiers include dates except year, medical record numbers, device
identifiers and serial numbers, and any other unique identifying code. For a patient
monitor, several of these bite in ways that are specific to the modality:

| Identifier category | Effect on this system |
|---|---|
| Dates except year | **The timestamp cannot be kept.** Continuous monitoring produces one timestamp per sample. Every timestamp must be generalised to at least day granularity, or expressed as an offset from admission. |
| Medical record number | Destroys the primary join key |
| Device identifiers and serial numbers | Destroys the entire device inventory, which is clinically necessary |
| Geography below state | **The bed is an identifier.** Bed 3 in a five-bed unit is quasi-identifying, so the location resource must be generalised, not only the patient. |

And then the observation that matters most for this design:

> **A five-bed unit produces high-frequency longitudinal data, which raises
> re-identification risk far above an isolated laboratory result. A patient in a
> five-bed unit can be trivially identified from their unique heart-rate trace alone,
> even with all eighteen identifiers removed.**

That is the substantive argument for **expert determination over safe harbour** in
this application, and it is the reason the design does not claim safe-harbour status.

### 8.5.3 The two-dataset split

The design keeps two datasets and never conflates them:

1. **The clinically operational dataset** — full fidelity, real record numbers, real
   device serial numbers, second-resolution timestamps. This is **pseudonymised, not
   de-identified**. It is access-controlled, role-scoped and audited, and it does not
   leave the hospital boundary.
2. **The analytics or research export** — identifier removal applied, exported as a
   bundle carrying a synthetic identifier, under an agreement that governs its use.

Keeping these separate is what allows a ward to run normally while still permitting
aggregate analysis. A single "de-identified" dataset cannot do both jobs honestly.

### 8.5.4 The DPDP Act 2023

Notified into force on **14 November 2025** alongside the Digital Personal Data
Protection Rules 2025, on a staggered commencement: core institutional provisions in
November 2025, notice and consent and data principal rights in November 2026, and the
remaining provisions including the Data Protection Board in May 2027.

The hospital is the **data fiduciary**; the patient is the **data principal**; a
vendor operating the monitoring system acts as a **data processor**. Obligations that
bear directly on this design include notice and consent, purpose limitation, storage
limitation, risk-based security safeguards, breach notification, and the data
principal's rights of access, correction and erasure.

> **A limitation worth stating plainly: the DPDP Act is a consent and accountability
> law, not a de-identification law.** It has **no safe harbour provision, no list of
> eighteen identifiers, and no expert determination route.** Its privacy model is
> consent plus fiduciary accountability.
>
> This design therefore does not claim that its data is "de-identified under the DPDP
> Act". It pseudonymises at the boundary, applies identifier minimisation in the
> spirit of the safe-harbour checklist for analytics export, and relies on consent,
> security safeguards and audit obligations as the operative controls.

One genuine tension is recorded rather than smoothed over: the Act's storage
limitation sits against **medical record retention governed by the clinical
establishments legislation**. These are different obligations with different
durations, and the longer one generally prevails for clinical records.

### 8.5.5 Security controls that are not negotiable

- ABHA numbers, Aadhaar numbers and one-time passwords **never reach a database or a
  log**. Encrypting a value and then logging the plaintext is the same disclosure,
  relocated.
- Encryption is performed in the hospital's own process. Routing a national identity
  number through a remote encryption service defeats the purpose; a value that has
  passed through such a service is treated as disclosed.
- The relational schema enforces the ciphertext envelope shape at the column level, so
  a plaintext identifier cannot be inserted even by a direct database write.
- Access is role-based, every access is audited, and the monitoring network is
  segmented from the hospital network and from the internet.

## 8.6 The build-and-verify process

This document is not only written; it is checked. A build harness assembles the
report, the schema and the figures, and gates the result on automated verification
before submission.

| Check | What it proves |
|---|---|
| Artifact presence and structure | Every declared section, appendix and figure exists |
| Standards linter | No superseded standard number is cited as current; no banned terminology code appears; each of ten deprecated-usage rules is enforced with auditable inline suppression |
| Terminology validation | Every code cited in a code span is a verified LOINC code; the unit-of-measure system identifier is spelled correctly |
| Schema execution | The DDL parses under a PostgreSQL-to-SQLite translation and loads with its seed data |
| **Behavioural constraint tests** | Fourteen inserts are attempted — thirteen deliberately invalid, each of which must be **rejected for the reason claimed**, plus a positive control on each table proving the negative tests are meaningful rather than failing for an unrelated reason |
| Index usage | The primary nurse-station query actually selects the composite index the brief mandates |
| FHIR resource lint | Every embedded resource carries its required elements, valid status and class values, and unit codes consistent with their display strings |
| Cross-references | Every figure is referenced from the prose, and no relative link is broken |

Two things this process caught that a human re-read would plausibly have missed, and
which are recorded here because they are the justification for having it:

- **A false-positive suite.** The constraint tests were initially reporting success
  while failing for an unrelated reason in every case. A positive-control test — which
  asserts that a *valid* row is accepted — was the only thing that exposed it. Without
  a positive control, a test suite that rejects everything would look perfect.
- **A data-formatting defect.** Enforcing that a row cannot be written before the
  moment it describes exposed that variable-precision ISO-8601 timestamps do not sort
  correctly as strings. PostgreSQL is immune, but any system that serialises to text
  — including a message payload or a national-exchange JSON body — is not, and the
  defect was in the design, not in the test.

## 8.7 Limitations

Stated plainly, because a design that claims no limitations is not credible.

1. **Clause-level numeric limits are absent.** The leakage-current tables, creepage
   and clearance distances, immunity test levels and alarm signal parameters are
   inside published standards that were not available during this project. They are
   omitted rather than quoted from secondary sources.
2. **The interface to real monitors is designed, not built.** Section 4.3 specifies
   the gateway and its responsibilities; no hardware was procured and no association
   was established with a physical device.
3. **The national-exchange integration is designed against documentation and a
   sandbox specification.** No live enrolment or publication was performed against
   production infrastructure.
4. **Usability has not been evaluated.** The controls in 4.7 are specified; the
   summative evaluation that IEC 62366-1 requires has not been conducted.
5. **No electrical installation was inspected.** The installation design in 2.7 is
   specified against the standard; it has not been verified on site.
6. **Waveform storage is specified but not implemented.** The relational schema
   deliberately excludes waveform data, and the time-series or object store that would
   hold it is out of scope.
7. **No mature standard profile exists for this data.** As section 6.5.2 records, the
   profile defined here is a prototype contribution, not an adoption of an existing one.

<!-- source: report/appendices/B_electrode_placement.md -->

Companion to `figures/m3_electrode_12lead.svg`. Covers the placement decisions the
figure illustrates and the limits of each configuration.

## B.1 Electrode types

| Type | Half-cell potential | Impedance | Motion artefact | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Disposable wet-gel Ag/AgCl | ≈ +0.22 V | Best, typically under 5 kΩ per junction after skin preparation | Lowest | **Default. The only type permitted in this system** |
| Dry electrode | Material-dependent; bare silver is +0.80 V and highly polarisable | Poor | High | Long-term wearable and home use only |
| Suction or cup electrode | ≈ +0.22 V | Poor transiently | Very high | Operating theatre only |
| Reusable limb clamp | Not Ag/AgCl; higher and less stable offset | Variable | High | Legacy. Not used |

**Mixing types or ages of electrode within one patient is prohibited.** The
half-cell offsets are common-mode and cancel only when the electrodes are chemically
identical. This is a stores constraint, not merely a procurement preference.

## B.2 Skin preparation

Intact stratum corneum presents roughly **50 kΩ/cm²**. Mild abrasion with a fine
abrasive reduces this below **5 kΩ/cm²** and is the single highest-value operator step
for artefact control — more effective than any filter in the signal chain.

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| 1 | Position the patient supine, arms at the sides, limbs relaxed |
| 2 | Identify the ten sites and mark them |
| 3 | Clean each site with alcohol and allow to dry fully |
| 4 | Abrade each site lightly — about 20 strokes |
| 5 | Apply conductive gel and attach the electrode with no edge overhang |
| 6 | Confirm impedance is acceptable before connecting the trunk cable |

Alcohol must be allowed to evaporate. A wet site produces an electrode impedance
far higher than the abraded figure, which is a frequent cause of a "lead off" alarm
that resolves itself after a minute.

## B.3 Standard twelve-lead positions

| Electrode | Position |
|---|---|
| RA | Right arm, distal clavicle |
| LA | Left arm, distal clavicle |
| RL | Right leg, above the ankle. Ground reference |
| LL | Left leg, above the ankle |
| V1 | Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border |
| V2 | Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border |
| V3 | Midway between V2 and V4 |
| V4 | Fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line |
| V5 | Same level, anterior axillary line |
| V6 | Same level, midaxillary line |

## B.4 The derived leads

**Einthoven, bipolar.** The heart is modelled as a point source at the centre of an
equilateral triangle formed by the three limb electrodes, and the bipolar leads are
edge differences:

```
I   = LA − RA
II  = LL − RA
III = LL − LA          and  II = I + III  (Einthoven's law)
```

**Goldberger, augmented.** The equalising resistors are removed and the exploring
limb is disconnected, leaving a two-limb average:

```
aVR = RA − ½(LA + LL)
aVL = LA − ½(RA + LL)
aVF = LL − ½(RA + LA)
```

The nominal augmentation is 50 %, but the measured ratio varies substantially both
between individuals and between leads in the same individual. **V leads and aV leads
are not interchangeable**, and the augmentation should not be treated as an exact
constant in any analysis.

**Wilson, unipolar.** RA, LA and LL each connect through an equal 5 kΩ non-inductive
resistor to a summing node of near-zero potential, and each precordial lead is the
exploring potential minus that node:

```
Vx = V(x) − WCT
```

For the precordial leads the central terminal omits only the right leg, so **the right
leg is a fourth physical electrode** and true unipolar recording requires all ten
electrodes present, not seven.

**The right leg is not an earth.** It is an active reference driven by the
right-leg-drive amplifier, which inverts the common-mode signal and returns it to the
patient. This is why the patient reference floats with respect to earth, and it is
part of what prevents burns at the electrode sites when an electrosurgical unit is
active.

## B.5 Mason–Likar modification

Relocating the limb electrodes to the torso — RA and LA below the clavicles, RL and LL
on the anterior axillary line — suppresses myoelectric noise during exercise or
ambulatory recording. The precordial positions are unchanged.

**The claim that this produces a tracing essentially identical to distal placement is
not supported.** Measured differences include:

- a rightward shift of the mean QRS axis;
- significant reduction in R-wave amplitude in leads I and aVL;
- significant increase in R-wave amplitude in II, III and aVF;
- altered precordial R-wave amplitudes;
- **inferior Q waves that may be masked.**

The last point accounts for the high false-negative rate for inferior-wall ischaemia on
exercise testing, and the inability to predict infarct location reliably.

> **Consequence for this system: a serial recording made with relocated electrodes
> cannot be compared with one made in standard placement, and the modification used
> must be recorded on the recording itself.**

Relocation is not used in this ward design; it is documented here because the hub
supports on-demand diagnostic recording and a clinician may request it.

## B.6 Five-lead at the bedside

The bedside configuration is **five-lead**: RA, LA, RL, LL and one precordial
electrode, conventionally V5.

| Configuration | Electrodes | Leads | Ward role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three-lead | 3 | I, II, III | Minimum viable; rhythm only |
| **Five-lead** | **5** | **I, II, III, V, V5** | **Selected. Adds ischaemia detection** |
| Twelve-lead | 10 | 12 | Diagnostic, on demand from the hub |

Five-lead is selected because it adds one electrode and delivers the single largest
gain in continuous monitoring: detection of ischaemic change, conventionally through
V5. Twelve-lead acquisition is a diagnostic procedure requiring ten electrodes, a
technician and a settled patient, and it is governed by the diagnostic
electrocardiography standard rather than the monitoring standard — which is precisely
why the monitoring standard's scope excludes cardiac monitors.

## B.7 Cable and connector discipline

| Element | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Trunk cable | 2.0–3.6 m. **Proprietary and not interchangeable between vendors.** |
| Lead wires | Chest approximately 74 cm, limb approximately 130 cm |
| Labelling | **AHA and IEC colour conventions are both still in service. The convention in use must be stated on the order, or the wrong leadwires will be delivered.** |
| Shielding | Electrically shielded throughout, entering a shielded compartment at the monitor |
| Defibrillation proofing | **Cables, not only electrodes.** A manufacturer recall covering tens of thousands of trunk cables worldwide was issued because certain sets reduced the energy delivered to the patient during defibrillation. |

## B.8 Applied-part classification

All ten electrodes, the patient cable and the lead wires form the **Type CF
defibrillator-proof applied part** of this system. This is the strictest of the three
applied-part categories because the surface of the chest is, in a patient with an
intracardiac catheter or surgical access, effectively direct cardiac application, and
because currents of the order of tens of microamps at mains frequency through the
heart can compromise cardiac function.

Section 3.2 explains why the electrocardiogram channel is isolated as its own domain
rather than sharing a reference with the other parameters, and section 5.4 shows the
corresponding leakage-current constraint enforced in the relational schema.
